# Dotfiles with agency: rules for agents working in this repository

This repository is public. Only public-facing material belongs in it; anything personal or tied to one machine
stays out.

## What never goes in

- Credentials of any kind: tokens, keys, cookies, passwords, `.env` files, auth stores.
- The owner's real email (use the GitHub no-reply address), real name, hostnames, and the names of private
  projects or repositories.
- Machine-local state: trusted projects or workspaces, hook trust hashes, approval allowlists, auto-mode
  environment blocks that describe a project, session or history files.

Instead, edit the live file and leave this repository's snapshot generic. If a snapshot has to follow a live
file, copy it, delete the machine-local parts, and run the check below. Approving a project, a hook or a
permission in a tool changes the live file only; nothing flows into this repository on its own.

## How files flow, and what to do

Nothing syncs on its own, in either direction. First find which kind of file you are touching: a folder's
README says "live" or "snapshot", and `install.sh` lists the live links (`LINKS`) and snapshot packages
(`SNAPSHOTS`).

| Kind | Flow | What you do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linked (shell rc, `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, skills, `mods`, units, `environment.d`) | The repo file is the live file; `$HOME` links to it | Edit it like any file, remembering it is public. If a tool or installer appended something personal or machine-specific, remove it, or move it to a local file the shell already sources (`~/.config/shell/secrets.local.sh`). Do not commit it. |
| Snapshot (Claude/Codex settings, git, nvim, ranger, rtk, opencode, desktop) | Repo → `$HOME` only, and only when the file is missing | Never copy a live file in wholesale. To follow a live change, copy only the generic part by hand, then run the check. `./install.sh snapshots` lists what differs. |
| Hooks and plugin entries | Repo → live, merged additively | `./install.sh --apply hooks`; it keeps the live file's other content and leaves a backup |
| Reference refresh (`agent-models/.../guide/`) | Generated into the working tree, uncommitted | Read `model-guide read maintenance`; source-check proposals before `model-guide refresh --apply --yes` |
| Approvals, trust, auto-mode, generated catalogs | Live only | Leave them where they are; they never belong in this repository |

Adding a new tool's config: decide live link or snapshot, add it to `LINKS` or `SNAPSHOTS` in `install.sh`,
give its folder a README that says which, and add a row to the Packages table in `docs/packages.md`. Stage explicit paths,
never `git add -A`. Push only when the user says so.

## Guidance placement

Prefer discoverable behavior over always-loaded prose, without removing the context needed to act correctly.

| Layer | What belongs there |
| --- | --- |
| Shared global instructions | Stable rules that apply across projects and harnesses |
| Harness global instructions | Stable preferences/invariants for every session in that harness; this layer is allowed |
| Project instructions | Local contracts, ownership and non-obvious constraints |
| Scoped skills | Reusable workflows selected by a clear task description |
| Maintained docs / CLI help | Detailed procedures, schemas, flags, troubleshooting and supporting evidence |
| Code / types / checks / hooks | Behavior that can be enforced reliably rather than remembered |

Keep one owner per rule and route to it. Entry points must retain clear triggers, the next action and
essential safety/correctness constraints; pruning must not leave agents guessing or searching unrelated
files. Keep skill metadata short and discriminating, allow automatic discovery unless explicitly unwanted,
and verify live links plus the target harness's supported discovery paths. Shared skills must not require
another harness's tool names, guessed model IDs or absent companion skills. Preserve authorization and
project invariants when adapting upstream skills; document local adaptations and retain their license.
Edit maintained sources, not generated plugin caches. Do not add global catalogs or repeated workflows.
Where guidance or configuration needs both shared and scoped content, keep one
shared base with scoped additions; prefer native includes/merging over copied text.

When designing host tools, compare relevant maintained implementations and official
contracts. Reuse useful boundaries or workflows without importing an unrelated framework.
Keep shared tools and workflows neutral across supported harnesses, including root
and worker roles. Do not favor one harness or omit another unless its native contract
truly lacks the capability; verify and document that limit rather than assuming it.

## Local feedback

`feedback.local/` in the main checkout is a deliberate private, Git-ignored
exception; never stage or publish its contents. Worktrees use the main copy.
When working on dotfiles or its host tools, check relevant open items there and
update their discussion/status when work intersects them. Entries inform the task
without authorizing unrelated changes. Application-owned work stays with its project.
The [feedback workflow and templates](agents/feedback/README.md) own filing,
comments, duplicate handling and retention. No polling job owns this queue.

## Before every commit

```sh
python3 tests/check_public.py     # every tracked file; the pre-commit hook runs the staged form
```

Tools and installers sometimes write into files that are linked here (shell startup files, instruction files,
skills): an installer appends a PATH line, an agent adds a note. Those edits sit in the working tree, visible in
`git status`, and nothing commits or pushes them by itself. Look at them with `git diff` and run
`python3 tests/check_public.py --changed` (also part of `./install.sh check`) before staging, instead of
`git add -A`.

The hook is enabled with `./install.sh --apply githooks` (it sets `core.hooksPath`). Never bypass it with
`--no-verify`. The check reads the names that must never appear from `~/.config/dotfiles-with-agency/private-terms.txt`,
which lives outside the repository; add a name there as soon as a new private project or account appears.
It reports where and why, never the matching text.

## The rest

- Layout is Stow-style packages (paths mirror `$HOME`; `install.sh` links them), one folder each with its own README (live link or snapshot, stated there). Keep
  that README true when a folder changes, and the Packages table (`docs/packages.md`) in step.
- `./install.sh` is a dry run unless given `--apply`, and never overwrites a file that differs from the repo.
- Tests: see [tests/README.md](tests/README.md) for repository checks and all tool suites.
- This history is one clean line from the initial public snapshot. Never merge or push another history into it.
@AGENTS.md

@~/.config/agents/AGENTS.md

## Status reports
- Routine status (worker/watch events, progress) is one line, no bullet lists. Save detail for findings, decisions, and final results.

## Delegation
- Prefer delegating to another harness. Use native Sonnet workers for taste-heavy
  UI/design work, or when other harnesses are out of quota and the user is away.

Read `~/.config/agents/AGENTS.md` before starting work and apply its shared
instructions alongside this file's Codex preferences.

## Command waits

For ordinary checks that may take seconds, prefer `exec_command` with a 30-second
yield. When only waiting for an existing command, use a 30–60-second poll within
the harness's limits. Yield sooner for interactive or background work; use
completion events for long waits. These windows do not limit command runtime.

## Background task notifications

Use the `codex-wake` skill when background command completion, a timer or an
external event should resume this conversation and no native completion trigger
already does. Read the skill before launching: it covers delivery preflight,
originating-session targeting and a background process that survives ending the
turn. Bridge watch already delivers its own events; do not wrap it again.
Notifications never answer a pending question or grant approval.
@[Shared instructions](~/.config/agents/AGENTS.md)

Shell commands go through `rtk` to reduce model input tokens and cost. Choose
command-specific filters; use `rtk summary`, `rtk err`, or `rtk test` for other
commands. Hooks rewrite commands where supported; otherwise choose the filter
yourself (`rtk --help`).
Treat unfiltered execution (`rtk bypass`, legacy `rtk proxy`) as a last resort:
raw output wastes input tokens and increases cost. Use it only for required
byte-exact protocol data or demonstrated filter breakage; identify the concrete
need before bypassing. A missing dedicated
filter, convenience or routine shell quoting does not justify proxy. Prefer a
safe filtered command or native tool; `rtk read --level none` reads full instructions.
Filter only output shown to the agent. Keep native, unfiltered commands where
stdout feeds another command: intermediate pipeline stages, substitutions and
file/protocol output. Let the hook handle rewrites; when wrapping manually,
filter the final consumer or the whole pipeline once. Preserve quoting,
redirections, `&&`/`||`/`;` and exit status; never pipe RTK's display summaries
into data-processing commands.
Bound reads/searches and recover elided content with `rtk recall` or a focused
read. Filtering/learning pitfalls: `~/dotfiles-with-agency/rtk/README.md`.
Prefer native harness tools when they cover the task. Edit/create files with
edit/write/patch tools, never Python, sed or heredoc scripts; shell is for
reading, searching and running commands.

## Scope and guidance

- Think first: identify the user's intended outcome and choose the cleanest
  supported path using the existing tools and environment. Verify assumptions
  before adding steps or switching environments, then proceed. Derive values
  from authoritative sources when reliable, honoring explicit choices; ask
  callers for a value only when it cannot be established from available context.
- Complete authorized work and proportional checks; preserve the objective
  across corrections and side questions. Reuse authority; ask only when the
  outcome or required authority changes. Reviews/explanations alone do not
  authorize edits. Finish or report the exact blocker.
- Read ambiguous replies in context and act on the most sensible interpretation.
  Ask only when alternatives materially change the result. Broad wording covers
  its purpose; keep narrow tasks narrow, preserve unrelated behavior, and stop
  when the acceptance criteria and checks pass.
- Necessary tool/runtime/dependency installs are pre-authorized when benefit
  clearly outweighs risk. Prefer user-local, pinned, reversible changes and
  report them. System-wide security settings remain out of scope.
- Apply instructions only to their scope; read supporting docs when relevant.
  User instructions outrank skills, subject to system/developer rules. Cite the
  file and clause if an instruction blocks work.
- Keep one owner for guidance. Shared globals hold cross-project/harness rules;
  harness globals may hold stable preferences for that harness. Put project
  invariants in project instructions, reusable workflows in scoped skills, and
  detailed procedures in maintained docs or CLI help. Keep discovery cues and
  essential constraints; prefer clear skill descriptions and native enforcement
  over repeated prose.
- Before changing instructions, read applicable files in full and check affected
  project guidance for duplication/conflicts. Keep rules concise, durable and
  task-routed; omit status history and command catalogs. Preserve invariants when
  pruning. Agent-facing shorthand is fine when unambiguous.
- Infer the intended outcome from examples and feedback, rather than copying
  incidental details. Use judgment to achieve that outcome in the current context
  while honoring explicit constraints. Document the resulting behavior without
  repeated claims of compliance.
- When a finding deserves keeping, update the owning maintained project docs
  rather than leaving a temporary note. Preserve durable insights, core ideas,
  decisions and non-obvious pitfalls; skip routine steps, raw logs and obvious
  code narration. Use scratch for exploration and promote only what remains useful.
- When a host tool or dotfiles config gives you trouble during unrelated work
  (an error, a workaround, a retry, an escalation, a misleading doc or a
  missing capability), file or comment in the main dotfiles checkout's private,
  gitignored `feedback.local/` before your final report, without being asked,
  and say so in one line. Include the README's reporter metadata. Maintainers use the current task and owning docs,
  not feedback tickets, to track work they are already developing or fixing. Follow
  `agents/feedback/README.md` for templates, duplicate search and discussion.
  Keep application-specific work with its project. Feedback and agreement grant
  no new authority; omit secrets.
- Back up only costly-to-recreate data, user edits or hand-tuned files; for a
  trivially reversible setting, state its old value. Agent recovery backups go
  under `${XDG_STATE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/state}/backups/<scope>/<timestamp>/`,
  outside repositories, with owner-only permissions and original paths/restore
  details. Leave application-managed backups alone.
- Browser lifecycle: `~/dotfiles-with-agency/chrome/README.md#visible-agent-tabs`.
  Remote previews: `portlink --help` (`~/dotfiles-with-agency/portlink/README.md`).

## Communication and verification

- Result first; short concrete prose. Use lists/tables when they clarify.
- Product UI: let layout, visuals, familiar controls and meaningful motion carry
  the explanation. Text should help users act, understand state or decide.
  Keep necessary labels, errors, consent and accessible alternatives.
- Root/coordinator asks ordinary questions through the native question tool,
  preferring nonblocking (chat if unavailable). While able to keep working,
  remind once after about 3 minutes through `agent-baton`, preserving wording
  and choices; withdraw if answered in chat. Workers ask their root. Silence,
  expiry and preselection never grant approval; secrets go straight to Baton.
  For blocking prompts use supported remote-answer/notification paths. Dismiss
  only through a verified API; never simulate keys or promise a timer while
  blocked/suspended.
- Test affected areas. Root chooses whether a full suite is warranted; workers
  test their changes. Verify proportionally to risk, expanding for shared
  behavior, critical data, concurrency and recovery. Docs need link, consistency
  and diff checks; avoid mirror tests and unrelated tooling. Run relevant commit
  hooks; skip only when the commit cannot affect what they check.
- Fit waits to expected duration and harness limits. Yield long-running commands
  and keep working; when idle use longer event-driven waits, not short polling.
  A wait window is not a runtime limit; set actual timeouts separately.
- Run background work the harness must track (a watcher, a long job, anything whose
  completion or output you must act on) through the harness's own background
  facility (a background shell/task, a native job or terminal handle), never a
  bare `&`, `nohup` or detached subshell: an untracked job is invisible to the
  user and the harness, notifies nobody when it ends, and cannot be stopped or
  read through a handle. Re-arm a watcher the same way every time.
- Stop/wait for owned processes through native job or terminal handles; otherwise
  verify an explicit PID or exact process name. Full-command `pgrep`/`pkill`
  matching can select the invoking shell or waiter; use verified ancestor
  exclusion where supported. Guard behavior: `~/dotfiles-with-agency/shell/README.md#agent-process-matching`.
- For a potentially recurring bug, name the failure class, sweep its affected
  area for siblings, and fix/report them together. Include the class in briefs.
- Fixture-only rules/thresholds are hypotheses: state the real-data check needed
  before shipping a fix. Before rejecting an approach on contrary numbers,
  check setup, data, sample size and tuning, try its strongest reasonable variant,
  and pause work built on it until there is adequate evidence.
- Optimizations need behavioral parity, not bit-identical output, unless the bits
  are the contract (hashes/keys, persisted identity, wire/crypto formats, promised
  reproducibility). A numerically equivalent change whose gains heavily outweigh
  its costs is pre-authorized: verify decisions on real data, measure the drift
  and margin to thresholds, and state the tradeoff.
- Visual changes require inspecting rendered output at meaningful states and
  widths. Check normal scale and dense/small details for clipping, overlap,
  spacing and legibility; tests alone and blind iteration are insufficient.

## Architecture and boundaries

- Inspect existing owners, vocabulary, codecs, types and helpers before adding
  equivalents. Import symbols under declared names; qualify or rename collisions
  rather than adding cosmetic aliases or duplicate declarations.
- Prefer one current implementation. Add backward-compatibility fallbacks,
  legacy paths/aliases or data migrations only when required by a confirmed
  production deployment serving real customers. For unreleased apps and internal
  tools, update affected callers together. Preserve validation, error handling
  and user data.
- Decode persisted/external/wire data once at its typed boundary; keep downstream
  APIs typed. Reuse equivalent semantics; update shared callers together and
  test parity/hostile input. Keep distinct domain constraints explicit. Reject
  truncation, coercion, ambiguity, invented defaults, non-finite values,
  timezone-less timestamps and other unauthoritative input; never add permissive
  fallbacks to satisfy callers or duplicate strict decoders in coordinators/UI.
- Keep code idiomatic and reviewable. Split oversized files at meaningful
  ownership/contracts; enforce a checked-in LOC budget where practical.
  Thin delegates need a real typed/protocol/framework boundary, lifecycle role,
  instrumentation, argument adaptation or deliberate public API.
- Apply type-checker quick fixes first, inspect the diff and rerun the check.

## Delegation

- Delegate only with explicit user authorization and when independent progress
  or scrutiny outweighs briefing cost. Use the `delegation` skill for coordination
  and native harness guidance, and `model-selection` for model/effort tradeoffs.
  Honor user choices; otherwise choose each worker's model and effort using
  current task evidence, supported native controls and allowance context.
- Use native subagents for same-harness work. The `agent-bridge` skill owns
  execution in another harness, model or quota pool; never bridge same-harness work.
- When root quota is nearly exhausted (user/harness says so), other-harness
  delegation is pre-authorized: hand off implementation, sweeps and reviews;
  root briefs, steers and verifies.
- Give workers clear ownership, constraints and checks; announce boundary
  crossings and verify their results. Delegation grants no extra authority to
  commit, push, deploy or mutate external systems.

## External APIs

- Before designing, changing, debugging or calling APIs, read current official
  docs for the exact product/version/endpoints and linked requirements. Establish
  auth/scopes, wire contracts, pagination/completeness, freshness, quotas/billing/
  reset, errors/retries and mutation/idempotency semantics.
- Separate published allowances, account limits/balance and local budgets.
  Discover quotas only through documented endpoints/credentials.
- Resolve uncertainty with bounded authorized read-only probes; record doc/live
  differences, reuse typed adapters, hide credentials and state unknowns.
  Documentation does not authorize paid operations or mutations.
- API reviews/delegations require the same doc check, citations and an explicit
  account of rules stricter, looser or absent versus the published contract.

## Task-specific guidance

- Substantial Python repositories: use the `python-project` skill for the
  baseline; follow existing equivalent tooling and use proportional checks for
  small scripts.
- `~/dotfiles-with-agency` is public: before editing/committing, read its `AGENTS.md` for
  live/snapshot ownership and excluded credentials, personal identifiers,
  machine-local trust/approvals. Stage explicit paths, never `git add -A`.

# OpenCode preferences

Shared instructions are loaded through `instructions` in `opencode.jsonc`.

# claude backend (Claude Code CLI)

- **Models**: `model-guide models --backend claude --json` reads resolved aliases and per-model effort ranges from native initialization without a prompt. Verify the worker's account and included allowance separately; a listed model can require paid credits. It spends the user's Claude quota.
  - Use it for taste-heavy work: UI/TUI layout and visual design (its taste beats every Codex model except Astra).
  - Also use it for work that needs live collaboration, or when Codex is out of quota and the user is away.
- **Sandbox**: workspace-write runs Claude's bwrap sandbox (writes limited to cwd plus writable roots, full network) with the auto-mode classifier on top. read-only denies edits and every command outside Claude's read-only set. Denials are logged as urgent.
- **Steers** land inside the active turn. Interrupt ends the turn and keeps the session.
- **Compact**: `agent-bridge compact <job>` resumes an idle session with `/compact`. It logs `compact_started` and, only on a `compact_boundary` event, `compacted` with `pre_tokens` and `trigger`. A successful result without that boundary is reported as `compact_noop` with Claude's reason; queued steers stay queued. This follows [Compact history with /compact](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/slash-commands#compact-history-with-compact) and the [CLI resume and stream flags](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference).
- Worker sessions stay out of the user's Claude resume picker and continue flow, while the bridge resumes them by session id. Nothing needs archiving. Workers load no user mods.

## Account selection

`cswap` manages native Claude logins; see `~/dotfiles-with-agency/claude/README.md#accounts`.
Inspect `cswap list --json`, switch an authorized account between sessions, then
run `agent-accounts refresh --backend claude` for the shared allowance view.
Bridge does not enable auto-rotation or map a global active account to every
existing worker. Verify the intended session's identity; do not rotate a login
under active workers or wrap Bridge launches in `cswap run`.

name: agent-baton
description: "Hand secret entry to the human without exposing values to the agent, or remind unanswered root questions through isolated forms. Use for login, 2FA, privileged prompts and human handoffs."
---

# agent-baton

A cross-harness CLI for human handoffs through Windows notifications or a phone over ntfy and Tailscale. Secret forms hold answers privately and type them into an approved app. Ordinary question forms return readable answers to the agent. These are separate modes: never collect credentials through `question`.

Requests belong to one conversation, which Codex and Claude Code supply automatically; on other harnesses the CLI's error says how to set `AGENT_BATON_SESSION`. Keep the returned request id for `wait`/`withdraw`/`type`/`forget`; never pick up another session's pending question.

Prefer native Baton MCP tools when available. Pass this conversation's owner on
every call: `codex:<CODEX_THREAD_ID>`, `claude:<CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID>` or
`explicit:<unique id>`. Never substitute a shared server id. Native `wait` checks
immediately by default; use the CLI in a background command for long event waits.
The CLI remains the path for composite forms, approved commands and `pass`.

For several ordinary questions or a disposable UI, `form <json-file>` composes built-in text, choice and select-many controls. `wait` returns answers keyed by question id; optional unanswered fields are omitted. This follows the same root-only reminder policy. The CLI help owns the JSON schema; do not invent an HTTP endpoint or supply HTML/scripts.

## When to reach for it
- For an unanswered ordinary question, follow the shared root reminder policy and preserve wording, choices and single/multiple selection. `question` supports free text and yes/no too. `wait <id>` returns JSON; `withdraw <id>` closes a reminder answered elsewhere. Cancellation/expiry is never consent; harness permission dialogs still apply.
- A page or app asks for an email, password, 2FA or one-time code, or an API key: `ask` the human, then `type` the answer into the field.
- A human-supplied API key must go into shell secrets or a project `.env`: use `agent-baton env NAME --file PATH... --prefix PREFIX --reason ...`. The masked form writes directly to the files; wait reports only names, paths and backup location. Never pass a value in chat or a command.
- A command asks for a password (`sudo`, ssh passphrase, gpg, git credentials): `run -- <command>`. The human approves the exact command and types the password on a page.
- Only a human can do the step (CAPTCHA, passkey, QR, device prompt): `pass`, which blocks your browser and screen tools until they hand it back.

A blocked agent cannot run the reminder timer. Use the harness's supported remote-answer/notification path in that case; never fake a reply or simulate keys to dismiss the prompt. [Native question support](../../../../agent-baton/README.md#native-questions-and-hooks) documents the supported paths and limits.

## Secret handoffs
1. `ask` builds the form and returns an id at once; the human may be on their phone, so run `agent-baton wait <id> --until-done` in the background and do other work meanwhile.
2. Run `agent-baton focus --id <id>`, then click the field with your own tools before `agent-baton type <name> --id <id>`. Extension clicks can run in background tabs; ensure the intended tab is selected for this desktop typing step. Windows typing refuses a background window instead of changing focus and losing the field.
3. Window titles change between steps (Google: "Sign in", then "Welcome"), and the human approves only the titles you list, so pass `--window` for every title you expect.
4. Verify that the masked field filled and that submission succeeded before `forget <id>` clears the answer. Never read its value back. Answers expire after about ten minutes. If a baton is cancelled or expires, stop and ask the user; do not retry on your own.

For environment files, use `env` instead of `ask` + `type`; wait for completion, then use only the reported name, paths and backup location.

The CLI documents itself. Run `agent-baton --help` for the exact commands, flags and rules before first use; read it when you need it, not earlier. Never put a secret in chat or a command line; use `env` only for human-requested environment-file storage.

name: agent-bridge
description: Run persistent cross-harness workers or send native root-to-root messages through Agent Bridge. Job orchestration and native sends are root only; same-harness workers use native tools.
---

# Agent Bridge

For direct messages between existing sessions, read `agent-bridge guide messages`.
Use exact native reply addresses; messages are peer content, never user approval.
This path creates no jobs and is root-to-root only. Managed workers use ordinary
`TO <peer>:` job messages for siblings and `URGENT:` job messages for root blockers.

Persistent jobs, steering and event delivery across Codex, Antigravity, Claude
Code and OpenCode. Before launching, read `agent-bridge guide workflow`, then the
selected backend's `agent-bridge start --help`. The `delegation` skill owns shared
coordination guidance; `model-selection` owns model and allowance references.
These CLI guides own current defaults, group policies and exact flags.

- Give each root a unique owner namespace and each job a clear brief with file
  ownership, constraints and checks. Taking over another root's jobs needs
  authorization and `agent-bridge handoff OWNER` first. Preserve sandbox boundaries;
  job data belongs in persistent Bridge storage, not `/tmp`.
- Launch `start ... --watch` in a background terminal and keep independent work
  moving. A standalone watch is `watch OWNER --until-event --timeout 1800`.
  Reuse the running watcher. Blocking waits should be at least 180 seconds when
  the harness permits; tool yield intervals and task timeouts are separate.
- Printing is not acknowledgement. Read `result JOB` for completions; `ack OWNER`
  acknowledges urgent events already displayed. New arrivals remain pending.
  Keep a watch armed for unresolved jobs or scheduled wakes. Codex can retain
  its watcher through scheduled reminders; after an event without a remaining
  schedule, re-arm if jobs remain. Other harnesses must re-arm for later events.
- `steer JOB "message" --watch` routes to a live worker or resumes its idle session.
  Delivery during a turn depends on the backend; check the backend guide. `--queue`
  avoids starting an idle worker; `resume` starts it. A live worker may consume
  queued messages. Retired jobs need `restore` first.
- Before changing a worker's model or login (`cswap`, `codex-auth`, `agy-auth`), look
  for `ctx=` on its `watch`/`status` line. It appears above 150k tokens of context; then
  read `agent-bridge compact --help` first. Below that, change freely.
- Verify worker findings and checks. Keep jobs useful for follow-ups and review;
  retire when their work is resolved and context is no longer needed. Purge is
  permanent; use the guide's retention/cleanup checks, not age alone.

For delivery troubleshooting, read only the relevant reference:
[Codex](references/codex-watch.md),
[Claude](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference#background-commands),
[Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/docs/subagents?tab=cli), or
[OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/docs/tools/).

name: agent-desktop
description: Operate Windows desktop apps and native dialogs from WSL using agent-desktop. Use for desktop UI inspection, form controls, menus, screenshots and native app verification; existing Chrome tools own browser page tasks.
---

# Windows desktop control

Run `agent-desktop status`, then read `agent-desktop skills get desktop` and
`agent-desktop skills get platform`. These bundled guides match the installed
binary; command help owns flags and the guides route to detailed references.
If missing, follow the [host setup](../../../../computer-use/README.md).

Use a fresh session for this task (`session start --help`), and pass its returned
ID through `--session` on every observation and action. Observe the exact app and
window, act on qualified refs from that session, then verify the resulting state.
Refresh refs after UI changes, including changes made by the user. Read
delivery/retry dispositions before retrying; an uncertain action may already have
landed. Do not switch drivers and repeat it without readback. Use Cua's installed
`describe` schemas when choosing that driver.

For screenshots, target the needed window or supported region without focusing
it. A capture reflects the window's current tab and content. If the user changes
the target before an action, observe it again and reassess the action. Use an
isolated renderer or headless fixture for layout checks that do not need live
desktop state; the [capture comparison](../../../../computer-use/README.md) lists
the installed drivers' options.

For WSLg windows hosted by `msrdc.exe`, avoid Windows-side move/resize through
either driver: Windows geometry verification does not prove Linux click alignment.
The launcher refuses these actions; read the [host boundary](../../../../computer-use/README.md)
when refused. A Linux-owned movement path needs separate validation.

Stay in semantic mode. Physical input, focus changes and `--headed` require the
user's explicit permission; a semantic failure does not supply it. Windows apps
can still raise themselves after semantic input: this was reproduced locally.
The Windows executable launched from WSL shares the user's Windows desktop.
Neither driver guarantees uninterrupted use while the human clicks elsewhere;
use a separate interactive VM or machine when isolation is required.

One coordinator owns a desktop workflow at a time, including any delegated Cua
steps. Driver command locks and separate sessions do not serialize whole tasks
or isolate the human's input. Do not launch parallel GUI workers on this desktop.

The launcher checks Agent Baton before every call, including screenshots. Use
Baton's secret-entry workflow for credentials; never put secrets in desktop CLI
arguments, UI snapshots or traces. While a human-only login handoff is held, wait
for its return before observing or acting. Baton still owns approved-window focus
and secret injection; desktop automation does not replace those checks.

For a visible demonstration, use the session's `cursor-overlay` with size `0.85`
(read `skills get desktop commands-system` for syntax). The overlay is separate
from the real pointer. At completion, end only this task's session to remove its
overlay and seal its trace; close only task-created apps/documents. Leave Cua's
shared daemon running. Keep screenshots/traces private; Windows file paths must
be deliberately mapped with `wslpath` before attaching local images to a harness.

name: agent-lab
description: Create, resume or retire persistent experiment workspaces outside repositories. Use for scratch work that must survive restarts, provenance tracking and experiment cleanup, with any harness or language; project code changes stay in their repository or Git worktree.

# Agent lab

Use `agent-lab --help` for persistent experiments. `new NAME --purpose REASON`
returns a unique ID and infers available session/model/effort context. Let the
tool detect it; supply overrides only when needed and known. Do not guess missing
provenance. Use explicit workspace IDs across sessions.

`path ID` returns `work/` for native edit/file tools. `run ID -- COMMAND ...`
executes there with a cleanup lease; `artifacts/` holds outputs and `tmp/` scratch.
The child receives their paths in `AGENT_LAB_*` and its own `TMPDIR`. Prefer the
created layout over new scratch folders in project roots or the home directory.

`show ID` gives provenance and size warnings; `list --sizes` finds larger labs.
Keep durable findings in the owning project's maintained docs, not a lab-only
note. Use `keep ID` if independent processes/manual work still need the files;
native edits do not acquire command leases.

When exploration is finished, `retire ID --summary OUTCOME` starts a 14-day grace
period; `restore ID` cancels it. GC previews by default and refuses live command
leases, mounts and Git checkouts/worktrees. Applied GC permanently removes only
eligible retired labs; the user timer uses the same rules. See
`~/dotfiles-with-agency/agent-lab/README.md` for storage, provenance and recovery boundaries.

name: arena
description: Compare parallel solution candidates and combine their strongest parts. Use when the user requests /arena, an arena comparison or competing implementations.
license: MIT

# Arena

Produce one coherent result from independent alternatives. An arena request
authorizes the requested comparison, not unrelated jobs or external publication.

## Frame

State the deliverable, constraints and a small concrete evaluation rubric.
Give candidates the same task brief and separate output locations, preferably
worktrees for code. Use the user's model/effort choices and the current harness's
available native agents. Without specified models, inherit rather than guessing
vendor-specific slugs. Load agent-bridge only when another harness is needed.

## Generate and judge

Launch independent candidates concurrently within resource limits. Each returns
its artifact and a short explanation of its choices. If one fails to produce,
assess the remaining candidates and report that limitation.

After writing finishes, use an independent read-only judge when authorized
resources permit. Give it the rubric and candidate paths; avoid disclosing which
one you favor. Read every candidate yourself and compare concrete criteria with
the judge's findings. Investigate disagreements rather than averaging scores.

## Combine

Choose the base a future maintainer can extend and whose constraints hold.
Inspect each alternative for useful parts; adapt those parts to the base's
contracts instead of mechanically combining incompatible implementations.
Convergence needs no forced graft. If candidates answer different questions,
clarify the brief before another round.

## Verify and hand off

Run the checks appropriate to the final artifact and inspect rendered visuals
when relevant. Resolve findings in the same owned scope. Preserve needed work
before cleaning temporary outputs/worktrees. Report the chosen base, useful
grafts, rejected tradeoffs, limitations and verification; commit/publish only
within the user's authorization.

---
name: benchmark-checklist
description: "Validate a measured performance claim or benchmark before reporting a speedup, regression or adoption choice. Check real work, errors, tuning, limits and repeatability."
license: MIT
---

# Benchmark checklist

Use this when you produce a performance number: a PR's before and after, a regression claim, a hillclimb harness, or a library or config choice. Answer each question with evidence from a run, not a guess about the code.

For a quick ballpark the user asked for, one run is enough. Still check questions 4 and 7, and say that it is one run. Skip the rest unless that run looks wrong. A choice between options is never a ballpark.

## Before you run anything

- Write down the claim you expect to make, in the words you would ship ("export is 30% faster at p50 on the 60k-row dataset"). The questions test that sentence.
- Read the measurement script. Note what it times, counts, and ignores.
- Check the load average with `uptime` and the core count with `nproc`. If the machine is busy, find out what is running. If you cannot stop it, interleave the sides so both see the same noise, and say so in the report.

## The questions

1. **Why not double?** Name the limiter. Profile in a run you do not report, because profilers and tracers slow the work down. Use CPU per process (`top`, `pidstat`), a runtime profiler (`node --cpu-prof`, `py-spy`, `perf`), I/O wait, and syscall counts (`strace -c` on Linux), then map the hot spot to source. Watch the load generator too: if it saturates first, you measured the load generator. If a change did not move the number, the limiter explains why, so find it before you call the change useless.
2. **Was it tuned?** Run every side the way production runs it: release builds, production flags and env, batching and transaction settings, connection pools, caches as warm or cold as production sees them, and the same versions and data. If one side runs on defaults, you compared configurations, not implementations. A limiter that is a setting (a commit per row, a debug build, a missing index) means that side is untuned. Tune it and measure again before you pick a winner. If you cannot tune it, do not pick a winner from that run. When the user is choosing what to adopt, narrowing the claim to the code as it ships today does not fix this, because they adopt the option, not today's settings.
3. **Did it break limits?** Do the arithmetic. Compare bytes per second with disk and network bandwidth, operations per second times cost per operation with your cores, and the time saved with the time the changed piece took. Removing a piece that takes 10% of the run can make the run at most about 11% faster. A result past a limit measured something other than the work, such as a cache, a no-op, or a bug.
4. **Did it error?** Count failures and non-success responses, and check that outputs are correct, not just present. Rejections are often fast, and timeouts and retries are slow. If the script does not count errors, add the count.
5. **Does it reproduce?** Run each side at least 5 times, alternating (A, B, A, B, and so on) so warmup, lazy initialization, caches, and drift favor neither. Report the median and range. A gap smaller than the run-to-run variation is no measurable difference. When the call is close, use a rank-sum test or the harness's own statistics.
6. **Does it matter?** Next to any micro result, measure the end-to-end path a user waits on, with realistic data sizes and concurrency, and report the micro result as a share of the whole. A helper that takes 1% of a request can make the request at most 1% faster, however fast the helper gets.
7. **Did it even happen?** Confirm the work ran inside the timed region: the request reached the server, the rows were written, the bytes were read, and the code used the result. Lazy code (generators nobody iterates, promises nobody awaits, results the JIT can discard) and timeouts produce numbers for work that never happened.

## Report

- Lead with the verdict: faster, slower, no measurable difference, or inconclusive.
- Give the number with its unit, the run count, the range, and the limiter. For example, "p50 41 ms → 33 ms, median of 7 runs per side, range 32 to 35 ms after, bound by JSON parsing on one core."
- Call the verdict inconclusive when you claim a difference but cannot name the limiter, when a side ran untuned, or when you could not check questions 4 and 7. Name the gap.
- Keep the primary result clear in a review or PR; link the supporting runs, range and limiter evidence.

## Other perf material

- Validate the baseline before planning a performance change, and validate later measurements too.
- For iterative optimization, make the harness report errors and completed work so each keep-or-revert decision checks correctness as well as timing.

name: blast-radius
description: Review what a change could break beyond its diff and prove the safety assumptions with real code. Use for blast-radius questions or a requested review of risky shared behavior.
license: MIT
---

# Blast radius

Find the breakage that a caller search alone will miss. Read the changed symbols
and connected code, including contracts the diff does not show.

1. Identify what changed and the one or two facts its safety depends on.
2. Follow consumers across persistence/wire formats, services, languages,
   lifecycle order, feature flags, configuration and pinned dependency behavior.
   Read the actual library version or local patch when the claim depends on it.
3. Give likely failures a concrete trigger, effect and source location.
   Distinguish confirmed risks from plausible but unproven ones.
4. Prove important safety facts by running the real code: a focused existing
   test, a small scratch repro or a live user path. A line citation supports a
   mechanism; it does not by itself prove the change safe.
5. Report the behavior change, proved assumptions, remaining risks and the
   cheapest checks needed before shipping. Cite cleared concerns when useful;
   do not pad the report with speculative callers or empty sections.

Evidence strengthens from a claim, to a source citation, to tracing why a bad
case cannot occur, to an executable check, to a live reproduction. State where
the evidence actually stops. Never describe an unrun proof as verified.

For broad changes, authorized independent review can add scrutiny; use native
agents or a requested arena. A review alone does not authorize product edits,
commits or publication. Keep public reports free of private details.

---
name: correct
description: Eliminate recurring agent mistakes in a repository through ownership, types, checks and focused documentation. Use for /correct or an explicit request to prevent repeated mistakes.
license: MIT
---

# Correct

Find the recurring mistake classes the user asked to prevent. Read recent
corrections, reverts, reviews, workarounds and instructions; cite the real examples.
A class needs evidence of recurrence, not a hypothetical error.

Fix each class at the highest useful level:
1. Give state/rules one owner, remove obsolete paths and prevent copying dead examples.
2. Use types or an actionable lint/check to reject invalid changes. If the
   pattern already exists, prevent new instances without forcing unrelated cleanup.
3. Test observable behavior. Prove the check fails on a real past mistake and
   passes after the correction; remove tests that only mirror internals.
4. Document only the remaining judgment calls, in their owning project docs or
   scoped instructions. Remove rules made redundant by enforcement.

Keep fixes within the authorized scope and verify affected callers. Exceptions
need a narrow reason and owner, with an expiry when temporary. Prepare reviewable
changes; commit only when authorized.

Report each class, its evidence, the enforcement selected and the verification.
Do not turn every operator correction into a new permanent global rule.

name: create-verification-skill
description: "Create a project-local skill that launches and drives the real app, captures evidence and cleans up. Use when asked for /create-verification-skill or a reusable app verification/control workflow."
license: MIT
---

# Create a verification skill

Every serious project needs a scripted way to drive the real app and prove behavior: launch it, exercise a feature the way a user would, and capture evidence. This skill generates that as a project-local skill (`<skills>/verify-<app>/`) tailored to the repo. `<skills>` is your harness's project skill folder: `.cursor/skills/` in Cursor, `.claude/skills/` in Claude Code, `.pi/skills/` in Pi, `.agents/skills/` in Codex, OpenCode, and others. If the repo already keeps skills in one of these, use that one. You write the generator's output for the next agent, not for a human: it will be read cold, mid-task, by an agent that has never seen the app.

## 1. Interview the repo, not the user

Answer these from the codebase and only ask the user what you cannot observe:

- **Surface:** what does a user actually touch? A web UI, a CLI/TUI, a desktop app, an API, a mobile app, a library? A repo can have several; pick the primary one and note the rest.
- **Run:** how does the app start locally? Prefer the repo's own documented dev command (package scripts, Makefile, README quickstart). Note ports, env vars, seed data, auth.
- **Drive:** how can an agent interact with it programmatically? Existing harnesses first — Playwright/Cypress specs, expect scripts, PTY helpers, curl-able endpoints, a debug port. Only then pick a generic recipe: browser/CDP for web and Electron, a tmux/PTY harness for CLI/TUI, plain HTTP for services.
- **Observe:** what evidence can be captured? Screenshots, terminal transcripts, response bodies, logs, exit codes, DB state.
- **Isolate:** can two instances run side by side (ports, data dirs, profiles)? If not, say so in the generated skill: refusing to double-drive a shared instance beats corrupting the user's session.

If the checkout doesn't build or start as-is, fix it only within the authorized task or report the blocker before generating; a skill written against a broken base teaches wrong steps. When an irrelevant missing asset blocks startup (a static dir the API never serves, a sample config), the generated skill may create it, clearly marked as verification scaffolding, and remove it in cleanup.

## 2. Generate the skill

Write `<skills>/verify-<app>/SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter (`name: verify-<app>` and a `description` that names the app, the surface, and when to reach for it — without frontmatter the skill never registers) and these sections, each grounded in what the interview actually found (no placeholders left):

- **Launch:** the exact command that starts the app for verification, and how to tell it's ready (a log line, a prompt). Launch must reach a usable state from an empty data dir, including any migrations and seed data. Ready means usable, not just that a process answers. A database health check can pass while its init scripts are still running. Include teardown. For a short-lived CLI or TUI there is no server to keep alive: launch means build the binary (or install deps) once, then start each drive in its own isolated PTY or tmux session.
- **Doctor:** one read-only check that answers "is this instance worth driving?" — process up, right version/build, port owned by us, auth valid. An agent runs this first whenever anything looks off.
- **Drive:** the harness recipe with real selectors/commands from this repo, not examples. Prefer stable handles (ARIA labels, data attributes, prompt strings, route paths) over coordinates and tab order.
- **Evidence:** what to capture for a proof and where it goes. State the proof standards: exercise the real user path, not internal setters or test-only endpoints; capture the action and the resulting state, not just the final screen; verify side effects (files written, rows inserted, messages sent) alongside what's visible; mocks only where a production boundary already isolates the external system. When the safe path is a dry-run or test mode, verify what it actually skips by observing (files, network, git refs) rather than trusting its name: some dry-runs still touch the network or open a browser.
- **Cleanup:** how to tear down instances the run created. Never kill by process name; kill what you started. Cleanup removes instances and scratch state, never the evidence: proof artifacts survive the teardown, in a location the skill names.
- **Helpers:** any script the skill ships is executable and its invocation is shown in the skill body. A helper the reader has to reverse-engineer is not a helper.

## 3. Seed the feature map

Create `<skills>/verify-<app>/features/README.md` plus one file per user-facing feature you can identify (aim for the top 3-5 to start, from routes, commands, menus, or docs). Follow the shape in [`references/feature-map-example/`](references/feature-map-example/), with a README index and one file per feature. Each file answers, from the user's point of view: what the feature is, how to reach it, how to drive it with the harness, and what observable end state proves it works. The four H2s are `Sub-features`, `How to get to it (user POV)`, `Driving it with <harness>`, and `Gotchas`. If the seed data lacks a precondition that a journey needs, the journey reports a failure and the reason goes in that feature's `Gotchas`. Never weaken the journey to make it pass. The map is the repo's maintained verification source; a proof that drives one convenient entry point is incomplete when the map lists others.

## 4. Prove the generated skill before handing it over

Run its own instructions end to end once: launch, doctor, drive ONE mapped feature (one is enough; the map exists so later runs can cover the rest), capture evidence, clean up. After cleanup, confirm the evidence still exists at the named location — a cleanup that eats the proof fails this step. Fix what fails, and run the generated cleanup after every failed iteration too, so broken attempts don't strand processes and ports. A generated skill that was never executed is a draft, not a deliverable. If you proved it in a stand-in for the real target (a container in place of a fresh VM, a local stack in place of a remote one), list every setup step the stand-in did that the target will not. Those steps stay unverified until a run on the real target covers them.

## 5. Offer the maintenance loop

Point the user at `/maintain-verification-skill` for keeping the map honest as the app changes. Suggest a cadence only if they ask.

name: delegation
description: Choose and coordinate native subagents or cross-harness workers for authorized parallel work, independent reviews and follow-ups. Routes briefing and lifecycle guidance to the relevant harness.
---

# Delegation

Delegate only work that benefits from independent progress or scrutiny. Keep
coupled work together and give concurrent writers disjoint ownership.

For model/effort tradeoffs, use the `model-selection` skill. The current native
tool's exposed models and controls take precedence over dated reference advice.
Choose each worker's model and effort for its task; set them explicitly where
supported. Use inherited/default settings only when they suit that work, not
because they are the default.

Choose the execution route, then read only its relevant reference:

- Same harness: [Codex](references/codex.md), [Claude](references/claude.md),
  [Antigravity](references/antigravity.md), or [OpenCode](references/opencode.md).
- Another harness, model or quota pool: use the `agent-bridge` skill. It owns
  persistent job launch, watch, steering, recovery and retirement.

Brief the objective, evidence/context, owned files, constraints, checks and
expected output. Name only supporting docs the worker needs. State whether it
may edit; delegation never expands commit, publication or spending authority.
A worker starts without your approvals, so restate any execution context the
user authorized and the work depends on (host access, a GPU, network), plus a
one-line check to run before bulk work. A worker never widens its own sandbox.
Use an isolated worktree for independent writers when they need one.
For heavy worker commands, the resource-admission skill owns host queue usage.

Keep useful independent work moving. Reuse a worker for related follow-ups;
start fresh for unrelated work or a heavy context. Match waits to expected work
and native limits: about 60 seconds for an answer, or 3–5 minutes for progress
when idle and permitted. Return early for updates. Workers report blockers,
coordination needs, actionable findings and completion; skip routine acknowledgements.
Cache policy belongs to harness docs; cache cost does not justify mixing
unrelated work in an old thread.

Verify claims against source and inspect the diff/check results. Small-model
output needs a root spot-check and an independent review before integration;
larger models still need verification, with independent review for risky changes.
Keep worker context while follow-up or verification needs it, then clean up
through that route's lifecycle controls.

# How

Trace the relevant source and explain enough of the subsystem for someone to
work on it. Match depth to the question: a narrow function question rarely
needs a full architecture report.

1. Identify the entry point, important types and the boundary the question
   concerns. Use the conversation to resolve a vague target and state your reading.
2. Follow the real call/data path, including callers, configuration and external
   contracts that affect it. Cite files and symbols; distinguish observed
   behavior from assumptions or unresolved paths.
3. Explain what triggers the flow, where state lives, important decisions and
   non-obvious failure/cleanup behavior. Use a diagram when it clarifies the flow.
4. Present the answer at the requested depth, with a short file map when useful.
   Skip empty sections and annotated-source dumps.

For a larger investigation, split independent angles only when delegation is
authorized and useful. Use available native subagents and current model choices;
otherwise investigate the angles yourself. The optional
[explorer](references/explorer-prompt.md) and
[explainer](references/explainer-prompt.md) templates preserve useful handoff
structure; load them only when using those roles. Read-only work stays read-only,
and findings must be checked against source before presentation.

name: maintain-verification-skill
description: "Audit and repair an existing project verification skill and feature map using source and live app coverage. Use for /maintain-verification-skill or a requested verification-workflow audit."

# Maintain a verification skill

A feature map rots the moment the app changes. This skill is the upkeep loop for a skill generated by `/create-verification-skill` (or any project-local verification skill with a feature map). The unit of rigor is the feature, not every sentence: cover every feature file from source and exercise every feature live, without terminalising every bullet.

## Outcomes

Pick one, and say which:

- **clean** — every feature got source and live coverage; no corrections needed.
- **changed** — a reviewed diff contains proven doc, harness or map corrections.
- **blocked** — coverage or a required correction could not finish. State the exact blocker.

## Edit scope

Only edit the verification skill's own directory (its SKILL.md, features/, and any harness scripts it owns). Never edit product code during a run: a behavior the map describes that the app no longer does is either doc drift (fix the map) or a product regression (report it, don't paper over it in docs).

## Pass

0. **Locate the target.** Find the verification skill to maintain: the project-local skill whose body has launch/drive sections and a feature map (usually `verify-*/` in the project's skill folder: `.cursor/skills/`, `.claude/skills/`, `.pi/skills/`, or `.agents/skills/`). Several candidates → ask which one; none → stop and point at `/create-verification-skill` instead of inventing a target.

1. **Index hygiene.** Read the feature map README and glob its sibling files. Fix missing, extra, duplicate, or dead entries. Lightweight; no generated inventory.

2. **Source pass.** Read each feature independently; use read-only subagents only when delegation is authorized and useful, otherwise perform the pass yourself. Each pass explains "how does this user-facing feature work?" from source, flags likely doc drift with citations, and returns one concise live-verification recipe. Children never drive the app and never edit files. Return shape: feature summary / source entry points / likely drift or none / one recipe.

3. **Reconcile.** Every feature file has a returned summary. Merge overlapping recipes into as few app states as practical. Spot-check cited drift; don't re-prove clean claims. Sweep recent churn for user-facing surfaces missing from the map — require a concrete source path before calling one missing.

4. **Live pass.** Required even when source looks clean. The coordinator owns all driving; follow the verification skill's own launch model — one long-lived instance driven serially for servers and UIs, or a fresh isolated session per drive for short-lived CLIs (the skill's Launch section decides, not this one). Exercise every feature at least once, and hold three invariants the whole pass, whatever the failure: (1) never drive an instance you haven't health-checked since it last did something surprising — doctor before first drive, doctor on each fresh session where sessions are the unit, doctor again after any failed drive, and where doctor can't see the failure (a wedged UI state on a healthy process), reset to a known state or relaunch rather than hoping; (2) evidence captured so far survives every cleanup, checked at its named location, not assumed; (3) nothing a drive started outlives that drive's usefulness — failed-iteration residue is cleaned whether the session is stuck, exited, or shared (for a shared instance, clean the residue, not the instance). A doctor failure caused by skill drift is drift: fix it under edit scope and retry once — restart whatever the fix invalidated, nothing more — before calling the pass `blocked`. A feature that can't be reached is `verified-unreachable` only with the concrete prerequisite (auth, entitlement, OS, external state) and the route attempted; if the map omits that prerequisite, that's drift. Any harness fix from triage gets re-driven live before it ships. Final teardown happens after the last drive of the run — including those re-proofs — so nothing outlives the run (evidence stays, per the skill).

5. **Triage.** Wrong or missing user-POV description → doc drift, fix it. Working behavior the harness can't drive → harness gap, fix it; a harness fix follows the same helpers rule as generation (scripts executable, invocation documented in the skill body). App behavior that's actually broken → product gap; record it for the user, keep it outside this maintenance diff.

6. **Hand off.** Re-read changed files and report the verified corrections and coverage. Commit, push or open a PR only when authorized. For clean or blocked, report the outcome without manufacturing changes.

Keep concise run notes (features covered, unreachable prerequisites, confirmed drift, outcome) in a scratch location; don't commit them.

name: model-selection
description: Choose a model, harness and effort using task context, native access, account constraints and current model evidence. Use for model comparisons or task-to-model selection.

# Model selection

Use the conversation and current session to make the decision. The tool supplies
execution facts and scoped observations; it does not choose through a leaderboard
or require a maintained per-model role table.

1. Establish the actual job: scope, ambiguity, verification, consequences,
   urgency and expected volume. Include account access, remaining allowance,
   competing work, required tools/modalities and existing session context. Use
   what is already known; distinguish constraints from assumptions. Continuing
   in the current session is an option when delegation adds no value.
2. For general model lookup use `model-guide suggest` or `--query MODEL`.
   When task-specific evidence would change the choice, add `--task "TASK"`;
   it suggests a focus and retains other evidence in `--json` and `--choice`.
   Check its fit; use `--domain AREA` only to limit the evidence when needed.
   It compares harnesses by default; `--backend` restricts one.
   Supply known constraints and task/session facts
   with `--context PATH|-` JSON; `suggest --help` owns the format. The context is
   per request, not a file the user must maintain. Native worker controls and
   selected-session access outrank a general catalog or cached account hint.
3. Use the compact comparison, which includes different access pools and
   observed quality/cost/time tradeoffs, then inspect `--choice ROUTE` when exact
   settings matter. Compare the relevant model/effort combinations and routes. Weigh likely
   usefulness against allowance, completion time, verification and rework.
   Read the reported reset windows, shared pools and model-specific limits;
   follow local policy drill-downs when plan conditions could change the choice.
   A remaining percentage or plan name alone does not establish capacity.
   Free access, higher scores, lower tier, newer releases and faster tokens do
   not independently establish the better choice. Keep source versions,
   workload, provider and harness scope attached; missing evidence is not poor
   performance. Public API prices do not measure subscription consumption.
4. Choose a concrete available model, harness and supported effort, or keep the
   current session. Explain the decisive tradeoff briefly. Name an alternative
   or a verification step when uncertainty could change the choice. Preserve
   explicit selections and do not change billing routes to get around an error.

Use `--query` for partial model names/families/aliases and `--json` for full
observations. Drill into relevant options rather than loading every provider's
catalog. `benchmarks` exposes individual source measurements; `read models`
explains their scope. When access, pool sharing or billing needs interpretation,
use `model-guide policy --backend BACKEND` for cached official policy evidence.
It refreshes missing/due policy sources separately from faster-changing model
and usage observations. Resolve a material mismatch against the selected native
session; do not turn a dated plan example into a standing eligibility rule.

Use validated cached evidence normally, with dates and source failures visible.
Research a material gap or changed contract rather than repeating general web
research for each choice. Fetched observations and reviewed guide changes are
separate; selection does not require approving a numeric proposal. Read `sources`
and `maintenance` before changing adapters or applying reference updates.

name: python-project
description: Set up or maintain the tooling and quality baseline for substantial Python repository work. Use for Python project development, packaging, CI and quality-tool changes; small scripts need proportional checks.

# Python project baseline

Read the project's instructions and existing configuration before changing tools.
Reuse equivalent tooling; do not install a competing formatter, checker, package
manager or runner just to match this list.

- `uv` owns environments, interpreters, dependencies, locks and execution
  (`uv run`). Do not mix ad-hoc pip, virtualenvs or lock owners; document a
  genuinely imposed exception.
- Use `ty` at the latest release, pinned exactly while pre-1.0. Replace an
  existing mypy/pyright setup at the same scope, fixing its findings. Enable
  opt-in rules that catch real bugs, not intentional boundary checks.
- Normal checks: Ruff format/lint, the type checker, pytest with coverage,
  Vulture or an equivalent dead-code limit, pip-audit and fast pre-commit checks.
  Measure before adopting xdist; cap workers to available host resources.
  Put slow coverage, audit, packaging and platform checks in CI.
- Each enabled tool needs checked-in configuration, a canonical command,
  deterministic CI execution, a pinned/locked version and a suppression owner.
  Suppress narrowly, with reasons, and prevent new unexplained suppressions.
- Small scripts can use less, but still verify meaningful behavior and reject
  malformed boundary input. A narrow fix does not authorize unrelated tooling
  migration; establish the baseline when the task includes that scope.

Run the affected checks using the repository's documented commands and inspect
their results. Do not add tests that only restate the implementation.

name: resource-admission
description: Run sustained CPU- or memory-heavy work through the host resource queue. Use for inference, benchmarks, dataset extraction, full suites or long-lived local servers; ordinary lightweight commands run directly.
---

# Resource admission

Read `agent-resources guide` before a heavy run. Declare the expected peak with
`agent-resources run --mem SIZE -- COMMAND ARGS...`; use measured needs when
available. Estimates coordinate admission and do not enforce a memory limit.

Never detach the command (`&`, `nohup`, `setsid`, daemonizing); the wrapper must
stay its own process. Do not wrap worker runners, nest admission calls or queue
ordinary reads, Git, edits, lint or targeted tests.
Use `--exclusive` for timing isolation only, never for test suites.

Start a run that may queue or last long as the harness's native background job
and collect it through its completion notice; a blocking call holds back steers
until it returns. Queue waits and root pauses are normal; inspect/report a dead holder or an
unpaused wait over 30 minutes. Root controls live requests with list, cancel,
pause and resume; workers ask their root. Keep inherited caps and sandbox rules.

description: "Edit drafts, README prose or explanations to remove AI-style filler and mechanical language. Use for /unslop or a request to make writing clearer and more natural."

# Unslop

Edit text to remove AI patterns. Scan for the patterns below, then rewrite. Preserve meaning and match the intended tone.

## Patterns to detect and fix

Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.

### Content

3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.

### Language

7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.

### Style

13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell.
17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.

### Communication artifacts

20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.

### Filler

23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.

### Jargon

26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. Pick the concrete word.

### Plain speech

27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number, and "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" and "leverage" become "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.
33. **Over-compression.** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read. "Parser rejects bad date → exit 2, no write" becomes "The parser rejects a bad date, exits with code 2, and writes nothing." Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs, and spell out arrows and abbreviations.

name: why
description: Investigate code history, design rationale, regressions or the evidence behind a threshold. Use when the user asks why a decision was made; use how for execution flow.

# Why

Answer the user's rationale question from evidence. Code shows mechanics, not
author intent. Separate direct evidence, supported conclusions, inference,
speculation and unknowns; [epistemics](references/epistemics.md) defines the tiers.

1. Identify the target files/symbols and the actual question. Follow relevant
   git history/blame, commit messages and linked PRs or tickets. Do not assume a
   GitHub remote, CLI login or external source exists.
2. Discover available connectors/tools, then search the sources relevant to the
   decision. A direct answer in a PR may be enough; a disputed or cross-system
   decision needs wider corroboration. Use the
   [source index](references/source-playbook.md) to select only applicable guides.
   Defensive code may also need its linked incident history.
3. Read the evidence in context, follow material leads and record the searches.
   Surface contradictions and missing access. Do not search every account,
   warehouse or chat merely because a connector is installed.
4. Synthesize with citations. Verify important claims and distinguish stated
   motivation from your interpretation. Test hypotheses in the user's question
   instead of adopting them. Name material unanswered questions and coverage gaps.
5. Give a concise answer for a narrow question. For a larger investigation,
   organize findings, alternatives, unknowns and sources; when a change follows,
   state what the evidence says to preserve, change or avoid.

Investigate directly unless independent source work merits authorized delegation.
Use the harness's available tools/model choices; no preset agent names or model
slugs are required. Give delegated roles only the access needed for their source;
investigation does not authorize writes or external messages. Optional templates:
[investigator](references/investigator-prompt.md) and
[synthesis](references/synthesizer-prompt.md). Keep their evidence discipline;
scale their sections to the question.

name: codex-wake
description: Codex host-hook task notifications, explicit event delivery, and recovery of a native worker blocked on an idle parent. Use for background wake delivery or diagnosis; Bridge watch owns its own notifications.
