# Codex task notifications

With the trusted snapshot hooks installed, launch background commands normally,
continue independent work, then end the turn when only the event remains. The
host `Stop` hook captures outstanding native command items and arranges delivery;
`SubagentStop` can recover an idle verified parent once per child turn. No wrapper,
hand-written message, PID or terminal handle is needed for these notifications.
This is event delivery, separate from Claude's visual Wake mod.
Verify installation/trust and live acceptance before relying on this path;
repository snapshots alone do not arm a wake.

| What will finish | Producer |
| --- | --- |
| Native completion already proven to resume this idle session | That native trigger |
| A background command or one-shot condition/timer command | Normal Codex exec; installed host `Stop` hook observes its native item |
| A native worker ending its turn | Native delivery first; installed SubagentStart/SubagentStop hooks recover an idle verified parent |
| A condition to watch for a while (a file, a service, a count), with several possible hits | `codex-wake monitor --ttl 30m --cooldown 5m -- PROBE` in a background terminal (exit 0 = holds, 1 = not); the host hook announces hits under its limits. Details in the codex-wake README |
| An event producer or an assigned logical result (analysis done, blocked) | `codex-wake send --message TEXT` once, at that boundary |
| Bridge jobs | Bridge watch; do not wrap it again |
| An unplanned worker blocked on an idle root | The recovery procedure below |

"Proven" means the idle session actually resumed, not that a message was queued.

```sh
codex-wake send --message "Analysis done: 2 failures need a decision. See notes.md."
```

Match a completion's native item ID to work already handled before treating it as
a new result. Read the private output file named in the notification. Command logs
start with a JSON context line, a blank line, then native output. Its captured text
can already be truncated by Codex. A command finishing, the notification
being accepted, the next turn starting and the logical task being done are four
separate observations. A worker told to report at a logical boundary sends once
there; that is a planned handoff, not the recovery procedure below. At delegation,
record the verified parent thread, the command handle/log, the expected event and
who acts next.

The observer uses native item identity, not an OS PID; `wait --pid` was removed.
Interrupt/session-end hooks pause delivery. Ordinary prompts preserve existing
observers across turns; a parent prompt after a pause starts a new generation.
Respect the interrupt control and any user pause. Do not infer permission
from a timeout. Async hook stdout alone cannot start an idle turn: these host
hooks call the existing task-message channel. Bridge watch and explicit `run`
producers must keep sole ownership of their notification.

If the hooks are unavailable, `codex-wake run -- COMMAND` is a fallback only in
an already-authorized context where delivery works. `--message` is optional;
it tees output to a temporary log. **Never escalate `run` out of the sandbox**:
that would unsandbox its arbitrary wrapped command. The agent-facing default
is normal sandboxed exec plus the trusted host hook. Retain a terminal handle
only to interact with or cancel a running command.

Explicit CLI producers default to the originating `CODEX_THREAD_ID` and `CODEX_HOME`.
Use `--thread`/`--home` only for an explicitly intended different target. `run`
notifies on success or failure; an existing event producer can call `send`.
Explicit producers preflight delivery; `check` diagnoses availability without
sending. A `PermissionError` means the sandbox cannot reach the control socket:
use the host hook or an authorized delivery-only call, never escalate `run`.
On delivery failure, inspect the command's outcome before retrying: it may already
have executed. A notification does not resolve a blocking
question or grant approval.

## Native worker blocked on its root

Use native collaboration messages first and continue independent work. If blocked
after two unanswered messages spaced over at least three minutes:

1. Identify the root from native spawn/parent metadata or the root's explicit
   brief. An inherited `CODEX_THREAD_ID`, a title or the newest thread is not proof
   of parentage. Do not choose another session when identity cannot be verified.
2. Read that exact root through the native task MCP's `read_thread`, keeping
   history/output bounded. Immediately before sending, confirm its reported
   status is `idle`. Silence is not an idle check; `active`, `notLoaded`, errors
   and unknown states do not qualify. Respect a user pause and pending human input
   or approval.
3. Use the same MCP's `send_message_to_thread` once, with the verified root's
   `threadId` and a short `prompt` identifying the worker, blocker and requested
   decision. Omit model overrides. This is the native task channel used by
   `codex-wake`; no separate wake process is needed inside the harness.
4. Verify the returned target and return to native messages/waits. Send at most
   one recovery wake per unresolved blocker; an uncertain receipt is not a reason
   to duplicate it. This never answers a question or grants approval.

For installation, producers and compatibility details, see
`~/dotfiles-with-agency/codex-wake/README.md`.

# Native Claude workers

Use the native Agent tool and its current schema. Native calls accept model
aliases; custom agent definitions can select a full model ID. Check available
aliases and effective model rather than assuming a family alias pins a version.
Choose effort only where the installed tool supports it; environment/settings
can override requested settings. A fork can have different inheritance rules.

Background workers have a narrower built-in tool set than foreground workers.
In particular, do not brief a background worker to ask the user directly or
assume it can use every root tool. Questions return to the root.

Use native messaging/resume for related work and native completion notifications
instead of shell polling. Keep the local Claude preferences for root and worker
selection; this reference describes mechanics, not permission to override them.

Source: [Claude subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents).

Watch the work · Use the tools · What’s included · Install · Packages

# agent-accounts

[← Packages](../README.md#packages) · **uv tool** · account observations

![Native observations preserve quota periods, pools and freshness. Due refreshes share a lock; Model Guide, Wake and Bridge read the cache, while Inbox uses its selected native connection.](../docs/images/account-context.gif)

Read account inventory without scanning jobs, messages or peer history.
The JSON contract carries account aliases, provider, windows, observation time
and freshness. Native window durations, resets, pool IDs and reported exact model
membership stay separate. Missing bindings/limits mean unknown, not unlimited.
Observations become stale after ten minutes or an elapsed reset. Addresses are omitted.

```sh
uv tool install --editable ./agent-accounts
agent-accounts snapshot
agent-accounts refresh --account a1   # explicit agy allowance refresh
agent-accounts refresh --backend claude # explicit cswap allowance refresh
agent-accounts refresh --backend opencode # existing native service, current directory
agent-accounts refresh --backend all --if-stale # refresh due sources for account displays
agent-accounts refresh --backend all --if-stale --max-age 120 # while the accounts are in use, a reading older than 120 s is due
```

Snapshot reads local Codex data through `codex-auth list --skip-api --json`,
managed AGY quota caches, and the last explicit Claude refresh under
`${XDG_STATE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/state}/agent-accounts/claude.json`.
Codex uses the versioned JSON v1 contract: source snapshot update time, refresh
status, actual `window_minutes` and Unix reset times. No plan label creates a
5-hour, weekly or monthly window. An opaque account-key hash preserves stable
local identity across ephemeral row numbers; it does not bind an existing session.
The current codex-auth projection does not expose metered bucket IDs or exact
model membership, so those fields stay unknown. Missing timestamps stay unknown;
old cached percentages never describe a window after its reset.
An API refresh failure is recorded separately from any still-valid cached windows.
Claude refresh calls `cswap list --json`; it can query usage and renew credentials.
Snapshots remain offline. Account displays explicitly request a due refresh in
the background, publish the cache immediately, and update again when it finishes.
Concurrent displays share a lock and source cooldowns; a failed provider or AGY
account does not block other sources. The cache keeps only numbered allowance
fields, excludes addresses and aliases, and expires freshness after ten minutes.
Claude's percentages are used allowance; this boundary converts them to remaining,
rounds down and never treats unavailable, elapsed or missing windows as free quota.
At a cached window's reset, its label and reset time remain but
`remaining_percent` becomes `null`: Wake displays `h?` beside any still-valid
weekly reading. The account becomes stale; old percentages never describe the
new window. The next due refresh obtains the current windows.
The active mark records the account at the last refresh; it is not session identity.
Native account selection stays in [cswap](../claude/README.md#accounts).
Named Claude scopes remain dynamic. The current cswap projection exposes a display
name but drops raw scope ID/kind/model IDs; the shared view does not invent exact
membership or duration for those scopes. Missing five-hour windows stay absent.

AGY accounts come from `agy-auth`. Refresh exports the selected credential to a
private temporary home and reads the native read-only `/usage` structured command payload,
preserving bucket IDs, period enums, fractions and ISO reset times. Rounded text
rows are not decoded. Distinct buckets remain distinct even when readings match.
Legacy text caches remain labelled as such until refreshed, with binding unknown.
An empty structured response cannot establish account availability, so it leaves
the previous cache intact and reports a refresh failure.
The observed native `/model` payload exposes the selected ID/effort, but neither
it nor `/usage` supplies exact pool members. Native pool names do not establish
model access. Bridge does not automatically rotate accounts or infer a pool or
cost tier from a model name.

OpenCode refresh uses the documented native `GET /api/experimental/usage/limits`
for the current directory, with a 30-second deadline and 1 MiB response limit.
It leaves credentials with the service. The private `agent-accounts/opencode.json`
cache stores a workspace hash, directory and normalized quota windows, excluding
workspace names, URLs and raw provider fields. Snapshot reads that cache only in
the matching directory and expires freshness after ten minutes; elapsed windows
keep their identity/reset with unknown remaining allowance. Null/signed-out,
unavailable, missing and malformed data never become available quota. Failed
refreshes preserve the previous cache, whose original age remains visible.

Go meters describe used workspace allowance, not independent remaining quotas for
each model or the free tier. Console windows retain the native spend-budget scope
(member/shared, set/per-model and covered provider/model IDs); missing per-model
counters remain unknown. Spend caps are not credits, and Go billing is separate.
No account or session is switched. The native service observation cannot establish
that a running standalone session has the same workspace or entitlement. Source
contracts and versioned schema: [model guide sources](../agent-models/src/agent_models/guide/sources.md).

Model-guide searches also use the provider context helper: quota observations
plus Claude's native auth-status plan/billing profile, with identity fields
removed. These hints are read dynamically, not stored in the benchmark snapshot
or hardcoded as model entitlements. Existing sessions can retain a different
account from the current profile.
Model-guide's separate `policy --backend BACKEND` command caches complete official
policy text on a slower cadence. The selecting agent interprets plan changes,
shared limits, paid-credit distinctions and opportunity cost together with these
native observations; percentages cannot predict task consumption.

Codex refresh uses `codex-auth list --api --json`; its native registry owns the
usage cache. Failed refreshes leave valid cached windows visible. Last-attempt
status is recorded separately and attached by stable account-key hash, so a failed
account never adds a warning to another account or follows a reused row number.

Refresh validates the selected account's result before atomically replacing its
private quota cache. It never switches the active account. Refresh without
`--account` queries all accounts in `agy-auth`. Claude refresh reads the full
managed inventory and does not accept `--account`. Errors do not include provider
stderr or credential data.

`agent_accounts.runway` turns repeated readings of one window into a depletion
warning. The caller supplies the readings (Bridge takes them from each harness's
own stream, or from this cache for AGY) and a history file, which keeps the rate
across restarts. A window is flagged once when it would empty within 30 minutes
and before it resets, measured over the last 30 minutes with at least two minutes
and two percentage points of movement, because quota changes in whole-percent
steps. The rate is the account's, not one session's.

Inbox continues to read allowance from the selected native daemon; a machine-wide
cache must not substitute for a conversation's account.

```sh
uv sync --locked
uv run --locked pytest
uv run --locked ruff check src tests
```

# agent-baton [← Packages](../README.md#packages) · **uv tool** (editable) · [Commands](#commands) · [Workflow](#workflow-overview) · [Questions](#unanswered-questions) · [Sessions](#simultaneous-sessions) · [Native questions](#native-questions-and-hooks) · [Phone](#phone-alerts-and-remote-handoff) A cross-harness CLI for human handoffs: ordinary questions return readable answers; login, code and password forms keep secrets hidden from the agent. A one-use page opens from a Windows notification or phone alert. State lives in `~/.local/state/agent-baton`. *The real toast and page, with an example site and fake values; regenerate with `docs/tools/baton_gif.py`.* ```sh uv tool install --editable ~/dotfiles-with-agency/agent-baton agent-baton --help # the workflow; agents read it when they need it agent-baton doctor # checks the toast, typing, hooks and the phone path, and says what to fix ``` ## Commands For native tools, register `codex mcp add agent_baton -- agent-baton mcp`, then reload MCP configuration. Other harnesses can launch the same stdio command. Every call supplies the conversation owner: `codex:`, `claude:` or `explicit:`, even when several conversations share a server. CLI and MCP select the same requests. | Native tool | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `question` | Free text, single choice or select-many; ordinary answers only | | `ask`, `env_secret` | Human enters secrets; `env_secret` writes to environment files without returning the value | | `status`, `wait` | Session state or answers; secret readiness without values | | `focus`, `type_answer` | Activate approved window, then type a held field by name | | `forget`, `withdraw` | Erase held answers or withdraw an obsolete question | Results contain `exit_code` and the existing CLI's `output`; exit 75 means pending. `wait` checks immediately by default; intentional waits are bounded to 30 seconds. For longer event waits, run CLI `wait --until-done` in the background. CLI still owns composite forms, command approval and human-only login handoffs. MCP adds no HTTP listener or global conversation state. - `question "Which scope?" --option "Current project" --option "All projects"` collects one ordinary answer. Omit options for free text; choices include Other. `wait --until-done`, run in the background, ends when the human answers or the request expires and returns JSON with `id`, `question`, and `answer`. A foreground call uses `--timeout 60` instead (exit 75 = still held). - `ask` builds a secret form (`name[:secret]=Label`); the human answers on a Windows toast link or, over Tailscale, on a phone (ntfy). `type ` then puts the held answer into the approved window at the OS level, through X11 for WSLg windows or PowerShell for Windows ones, and refuses terminals and agent windows. Use `focus --id ` before selecting the field: extension actions can target background tabs, while desktop typing needs the intended tab selected. Windows typing preserves field focus and refuses a background window, missing payload, or rejected keyboard input. - `env LIQUID_API_KEY --prefix liquid_ --file ~/.config/shell/secrets.local.sh --file .env --reason "Configure the API client"` asks the human for a masked value and stores it directly in those files. Shell files use `export`, other files use plain `NAME=value`; matching entries are replaced. Existing files are backed up with restore paths under `$XDG_STATE_HOME/backups/env-secrets/`, and targets end with mode `0600`. Symlinked and group/world-writable targets are refused. `wait ` reports only the name, paths and backup location. - `run -- ` lets the human approve the exact command and type a password on a page (sudo, ssh, gpg). - `pass ` is for steps only a human can do (CAPTCHA, passkey): browser and screen tools stay blocked until they hand it back. - `agent-baton guard` is the `PreToolUse` hook that does the blocking; `install.sh --apply hooks` adds it to the Claude and Codex configs. The [agent-desktop launcher](../computer-use/README.md) also checks it on every call, including in harnesses without those hooks. Its exact `guard` entrypoint loads only guard dependencies, keeping the per-tool path independent of web-page, notification and secret-injection startup. CLI/help and guard verdicts remain covered by the same command contracts. ## Workflow overview ![Three handoff paths: a worker's decision returns through its root, concurrent sessions receive their own replies, and secrets reach an approved app or command.](../docs/images/bridge-baton-scenes.gif) With [Agent Bridge](../agent-bridge/README.md#when-a-worker-needs-you), the root connects worker state to the human handoff, then steers or resumes the right job. The picture shows the root's coordination steps; it does not imply an automatic relay. The sections below give each path's rules. ## Unanswered questions | Question type | CLI | Returned `answer` | | --- | --- | --- | | Free text, including multiline | `question "What should change?"` | String | | Yes/no or explicit approval | `question "Proceed?" --option "Yes, proceed" --option "No"` | String | | Single choice | `question "Scope?" --option "Local" --option "Shared"` | String | | Select all that apply | `question "Platforms?" --multiple --option "Linux" --option "Windows"` | List of strings | Choice forms include Other with a written answer. Select-many results follow the listed option order, then Other if provided. Nothing is preselected. Each call collects one question; mandatory harness permission dialogs still apply. For several questions or a one-off UI, agents can use the CLI JSON interface: ```sh agent-baton form examples/review-form.json agent-baton wait --timeout 60 ``` The [example definition](examples/review-form.json) mixes single choice, select-many and optional text fields. `wait` returns `{"id":"...","title":"...","answers":{...}}`, keyed by field id. Agents can write their own temporary definition with the same schema; `agent-baton --help` owns its fields and limits. Forms expire and can be withdrawn like individual questions. This adds no public HTTP API or arbitrary HTML/JS. When the root remains active: ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Root asks through native harness] --> B{Answered within 3 minutes?} B -->|Yes| C[Continue work] B -->|No| D[One Baton notification] D --> E[Phone or PC: choose or write] E --> F[wait returns answer to root] ``` The shared instructions apply this reminder policy to any harness: native question tool first, chat if unavailable, then one Baton reminder after about three minutes. Workers report questions to the root; only the root notifies the human. Keep the question and options unchanged, and keep independent work moving. If the human answers in chat first, `agent-baton withdraw ` closes the stale form. Silence, decline, expiry and defaults never grant approval. The active agent tracks the delay; this is not a background timer or harness hook. A suspended agent or blocking native question tool cannot trigger a timed reminder. The CLI accepts calls from any harness; `AGENT_BATON_BY` can name it in the form. ### Simultaneous sessions Each request records its conversation owner, has its own Windows notification tag and one-use reply link. Answering B leaves A pending. `wait`, `withdraw`, `type`, `forget`, `status` and same-site login reuse stay within the caller's session, even when an explicit request id is supplied. Ambiguous secret typing requires `--id`. Codex (`CODEX_THREAD_ID`) and Claude Code (`CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`) are identified automatically. For any other harness, choose a unique, nonsecret conversation id once and pass `AGENT_BATON_SESSION` on **every** call (it also overrides the automatic id): ```sh AGENT_BATON_SESSION=conversation-UUID agent-baton question "Which scope?" AGENT_BATON_SESSION=conversation-UUID agent-baton wait --timeout 60 ``` Replace the placeholder with the same unique value for this conversation only; never put a shared session value in shell startup. `AGENT_BATON_BY` is only a display name. Missing identity fails closed; old requests without an owner are never adopted. Their original human pages still work; standalone human CLI calls need the originating session context. `doctor`, `windows` and `guard` need none. The phone can keep one shared ntfy topic: each notification opens its own form. Concurrent phone requests need enough forwarded `slots`; overflow stays local. The login screen lock remains global because agents share the physical screen; ordinary questions do not lock it. This prevents accidental session crossover, not access by an untrusted process running under the same OS account. ### Native questions and hooks Prefer a nonblocking native question tool when the harness exposes one. A hook's own timeout limits the hook process; it does not set a deadline on the question. No native-question cancellation hook or background watcher is installed here. | Harness | Supported path | | --- | --- | | Codex | Use the asynchronous native question tool when available. Background hook output cannot control an already-running operation or start an idle turn. [OpenAI hooks reference](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks#run-hooks-in-the-background). | | Claude Code | Use Remote Control and mobile input-needed alerts for native questions; the [configuration snapshot](../claude/README.md#remote-questions-and-notifications) enables both. Inbox cannot answer them. `dialogExpiry` applies to other dialogs. [Remote Control reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control#limitations). | | OpenCode | Its native `question` pauses execution. The v2 API can list and cancel pending forms with feedback, but this requires a dedicated adapter with root-session filtering and answer/cancellation race handling. [Tools](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/tools/), [API](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/api). | | Antigravity | Hooks can intercept `ask_question` before execution. The documented hook contract provides no cancellation of an already-open question. Use the native prompt or supported remote interface. [Hooks reference](https://antigravity.google/docs/hooks). | An active root can use Baton's reminder flow above. A blocked root must rely on the native answer path; no timer is promised in that state. Automatic handoff requires a verified per-harness adapter before it can be enabled. Never use synthetic keystrokes, invented answers or permission auto-approval as a timeout. Ordinary answers are shared with the model and saved locally in files with mode `0600`. Resolved state is removed on a later launch after about a day. Never enter credentials into ordinary questions or forms; use `ask`, `env`, or `run`, whose secret answers stay in daemon memory until typed or stored. ## Phone alerts and remote handoff ```mermaid flowchart LR request["Agent needs input"] --> desktop["Windows toast"] request --> phone["Phone push (optional)
ntfy: urgent"] desktop --> form["You answer
One-use form"] phone -->|"Encrypted Tailscale tunnel"| form ``` With phone routing configured, requests also send an ntfy push with a link to the one-use form at [maximum priority (`5` / `urgent`)](https://docs.ntfy.sh/publish/#message-priority). Subscribe to the private topic in the phone app and allow notifications; sound, vibration and pop-up behavior still depend on the phone's notification settings. Optional settings go in `~/.config/agent-baton/config.toml` (untracked): `ntfy` (a private topic URL), `url` (a Tailscale IP such as `http://100.x.y.z`) and `port` for phone alerts, then `tailscale serve --bg --tcp=80 tcp://127.0.0.1:`; `slots` raises how many open requests get their own phone port. The [Tailscale Serve tunnel](https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/tailscale-cli/serve) lets you answer away from the PC over an encrypted connection within your tailnet. Keep the host reachable and Tailscale connected on both devices. The IP route avoids Android secure-DNS trouble with `.ts.net` names. A fixed forwarded port can serve only one open request at a time; further requests are local-only. Run `agent-baton doctor` after setup. The push to the phone carries no detail, only "needs you"; what and why are on the page. Checks (from this directory): ```sh uv sync --locked uv run --locked pytest uv run --locked ruff check src tests ```

# agent-bridge

[← Packages](../README.md#packages) · **uv tool** (editable) · [Install](#install) · [Direct messages](#direct-session-messages) · [When a worker needs you](#when-a-worker-needs-you) · [Restore](#restore-and-root-access) · [Model references](#model-references)

A cross-harness CLI that lets a root coding agent (Codex, Antigravity/agy, Claude Code or OpenCode) hand work to workers of
the other harnesses: start a job from a written brief, watch it live, steer or interrupt it, and review its result.
Keep the job for related follow-ups; retire it only when its work is resolved and its context is no longer needed.
`retire <owner>/<name>` archives the report and hides the job, keeping its data in place for
14 days by default (`--keep-days N`). `restore <owner>/<name>` makes it active again, and
`resume` continues the original thread/session. `purge` deletes expired retired jobs only
when explicitly run; `retire --purge` deletes immediately. Both keep archived reports readable
with `result`, but purged sessions cannot be restored. See `agent-bridge guide workflow`.
Jobs persist under `~/.local/state/agent-bridge`, so another root can resume or take over, and
workers can message each other with `TO <peer>:`. Plain worker messages, including ones addressed `TO root:`,
go to the coordinator as info.

`agent-bridge message` adds direct native messages between independent root sessions,
without creating jobs or taking over another root's workers. Read
`agent-bridge guide messages` for discovery, reply addresses, native transports,
native API setup and receipt limits. It uses agent-message APIs, with no user-chat
fallback. The job lifecycle and existing worker delivery remain unchanged.

To take over an existing owner namespace from a different known root, run
`agent-bridge handoff <owner>` once from the new root. The previous root can
still inspect shared status, but its job mutations, acknowledgements and watch
delivery are refused after the handoff. Unknown/rootless callers retain legacy
access without replacing a known binding.

`agent-bridge steer <owner>/<name> "follow-up"` delivers to a running worker, or
resumes an idle job detached in its original session. Add `--watch` to follow the
new work in the same background command. Use `--queue` to batch messages without
starting an idle job, then `resume` to deliver them in order. Retired jobs require
`restore` first. Watching alone never starts work.

`agent-bridge sessions` exports a versioned JSON inventory of native worker IDs
across all owners and backends, excluding retired jobs, for tools such as [Agent Inbox](../agent-inbox/README.md).
It contains job identity and recorded launcher metadata, never prompts, credentials
or account settings. New jobs record a parent when the root exposes its native
session ID. Other harnesses can supply `AGENT_BRIDGE_ROOT_HARNESS` and
`AGENT_BRIDGE_ROOT_SESSION` for that invocation; older jobs keep an unspecified
parent rather than guessing one. Workers cannot export other owners' inventory.

![The root delegates work across harnesses and verifies persistent job results. A separate native messaging path connects existing Codex, Claude Code, agy and OpenCode sessions by exact address, steering where supported without creating jobs or granting approval.](../docs/images/agent-bridge-flow.gif)

In Claude Code, [Wake](../claude/README.md#crew-and-quota-rows) draws these jobs as crew, with
worker/model/effort labels and an account quota row.

Claude workers observe their main agent's effort through native PostToolUse and Stop hooks.
Until a hook reports it, the effective effort is unknown; the requested effort remains separate.
Hook values describe the setting observed at that event, which can precede a pending change taking effect.

Every harness can use the same versioned object:

```sh
agent-bridge status --json                 # jobs, pressure, quota caches and peer graph
agent-bridge status --json <owner>         # owner or owner/job filter
agent-bridge status --json --storage       # also verify expired retirement and sizes
agent-bridge guide status
```

The [status guide](src/agent_bridge/guide/status.md) documents fields, polling,
unknown readings and additive V1 evolution. The checked-in
[JSON Schema](src/agent_bridge/status.schema.json) ships with the package.
Readers ignore unknown fields and reject unsupported `schema_version` values.
`owners` and `watch` share the job-status producer. Wake's account row reads
`agent-accounts` independently; peer
edges include stable IDs, direction, counts and last-activity timestamps.
Poll about every ten seconds, with storage scans on demand. Reading status never
acknowledges events. A streaming diff mode awaits a reliable cross-source cursor
protocol.

## Direct session messages

Ask another active session for a review, share a finding or coordinate a shared
resource through its native agent-message API:

```sh
agent-bridge message whoami
agent-bridge message list
agent-bridge message send claude:NATIVE_ID --text 'Can you review the shared change?'
agent-bridge guide messages
```

This path is available to roots in all four harnesses. Native sends from managed
workers are rejected by both the CLI and import API. Workers use `TO <peer>:` job
messages for siblings and `URGENT:` job messages for root blockers; these channels
need no native session discovery. Use the exact native recipient address. Steering is used where
the native API supports it; a send receipt does not prove the message was read.
Messages remain peer content and grant no user approval. The
[messaging guide](src/agent_bridge/guide/messages.md) owns setup and transport limits.

## When a worker needs you

Choose a group policy when launching several workers. Default `each` batches
completions for 60 seconds; `all` waits for the group (optionally `--max-wait`),
and `quiet` leaves results visible. `group set OWNER NAME --wake all --members a b`
configures a group; launch with `--group NAME`. Unread results wake the root once
after 15 minutes by default, including under `quiet`, when a watch remains armed
in every harness. Reminders are observation-driven; without an armed watch, there
is no background push.
The [group contract](src/agent_bridge/guide/status.md#completion-groups-v11)
documents controls and fields. `watch --until-event` delivers completion digests
once and immediately wakes for failures, questions, errors and explicit
blocking/URGENT messages, flushing any held results.
In a Codex root, the watch process sends wake events, timeouts and failures through
the shared [Codex Wake client](../codex-wake/README.md) and the current thread's
native MCP tool, including after the model turn ends. Empty
handled owners exit silently. After its first wake, it remains alive through
scheduled unread reminders and group completions, even with no runners; this may
outlast `--timeout`. Re-arm after an event if a job remains but no schedule is
pending. Other roots still need to re-arm their watch for reminders. A short
startup line confirms delivery is ready; the root needs no separate callback.
Routine messages and slow/stall notices remain visible; `--include-info` also
wakes for them. Group policies still apply with that flag; overdue unread
reminders wake without it. Queue waits and retry status never wake the root.
Re-arming cannot discard a completion. Printing is not acknowledgement:
`agent-bridge result <owner>/<job>` acknowledges that job's completions for roots.
Workers read peer results without taking the root lock or acknowledging them.
`agent-bridge ack <owner>` (or `<owner>/<job>`) acknowledges urgent events already
displayed by watch. Handle questions and errors before acknowledging them. New
events arriving after display stay pending. Use a unique owner per root; its
versioned `jobs/<owner>/ack.json` stores per-job byte cursors, with locked atomic
updates. Missing cursors replay old urgent history; old jobs need no migration.
See `agent-bridge guide workflow` for the cursor format and watch lifecycle.
A Claude worker that the runtime quietly served with a different model than the one it
resolved to (a fallback; the stream still reports the requested model) raises one urgent
`model_fallback` event per job and served model, naming both and saying the worker was not
told. Bridge compares successive per-model usage totals to find the output for that turn;
the model that wrote most of it must differ from the resolved one, so a small helper model
never counts. The first result after a resume establishes a baseline and cannot identify a fallback.
A sandboxed worker's `agent-bridge waiting` cannot take the job's state lock; it leaves
its declaration in `out/.waiting.json` instead, which status reads (the newer of the two
wins, and the next activity clears it), without widening what the worker may write.
Wake shows names first with compact event ages, marks classifier-assessed silence as
`stalled`, and keeps unacknowledged completions visible as `done`. Known turn
times appear only when useful and space allows.

Workers report questions to their root. The root asks through its native harness,
then uses [Baton](../agent-baton/README.md#unanswered-questions) for one reminder
after about three minutes if it remains active. It reads the answer and explicitly
steers or resumes the relevant Bridge job; no automatic question relay is installed.
Independent jobs can keep running while a decision is pending. Permission and
approval requirements still apply. Baton's
[workflow overview](../agent-baton/README.md#workflow-overview) diagrams this path.

## Install

Install and use (a uv tool, editable from this checkout):

```sh
uv tool install --with-editable ~/dotfiles-with-agency/codex-wake \
  --with-editable ~/dotfiles-with-agency/agent-models --with-editable ~/dotfiles-with-agency/agent-resources \
  --with-editable ~/dotfiles-with-agency/agent-accounts --editable ~/dotfiles-with-agency/agent-bridge
agent-bridge --help            # compact command map and workflow rules
agent-bridge guide workflow    # Bridge routing, watching, steering and cleanup
model-guide read models       # generic model strength, effort and costs
model-guide read subscriptions # all vendor tiers; read only for plan-dependent choices
agent-bridge start --help      # each backend's models, effort levels, quota and quirks
```

The documentation is the `guide` and per-command `--help` output on purpose, so a model reads it when it decides to rather than
carrying it in every prompt. It is assembled from `src/agent_bridge/guide/*.md`; the skill in
`agents/.agents/skills/agent-bridge/` is only a short briefing.

Notes:
- **Sandboxes are never bypassed.** Workers run in a systemd scope with memory and CPU caps; OpenCode runs
  under `bwrap`, and only the zero-retention free models are allowed.
- **A worker cannot start jobs**: it carries `AGENT_BRIDGE_WORKER`, which the CLI refuses.
- **Reference updates:** `model-guide read maintenance` owns the review workflow.

Checks (from this directory):

```sh
uv sync --locked
uv run --locked pytest
uv run --locked ruff check src tests
```

## Resource integration

[Agent resources](../agent-resources/README.md) owns host admission, queue controls
and cancellation. Bridge injects the worker/job/controller identity, shares the
queue through OpenCode's sandbox mount, and reports waits and pressure without
waking the root. Workers use `agent-resources run --mem SIZE -- <command>`.
The queue preserves the already-filtered worker environment and existing caps.

Choose job caps with `start ... --memory 4G --cpu 400%`, or `resume <job>` with
those flags for its next launch. Caps above effective slice/host budgets are
refused. A plain resume sends `Continue.` in the same native session when no
steers are queued. Transient backend failures get four bounded, jittered retries
on the same model; exhaustion suggests resuming that same thread on another model.

## Worker environment

Worker launches remove variables whose names contain `KEY`, `TOKEN`, `SECRET`,
`PASSWORD`, `CREDENTIAL`, `AUTH` or `COOKIE` (case-insensitive). Normal runtime,
locale, proxy and backend config paths remain available; existing backend auth
files are unchanged. Set `AGENT_BRIDGE_PASS_ENV=NAME1,NAME2` in the root environment
to pass specific variables a job needs. `AGENT_BRIDGE_DENY_ENV=NAME1,NAME2` adds
exact names to remove, taking precedence over pass-through. Lists use exact,
case-sensitive names and reject wildcards or malformed entries without echoing
their contents.

The filter applies at Bridge worker/helper launch. Standalone resource commands
preserve their caller's environment; account queries use their own selected login. Set pass-through before launching a worker: a removed variable
cannot be recovered from its parent environment later. Variables such as
`SSH_AUTH_SOCK` also match the default filter and need explicit pass-through
when required. This filters inherited environments; it does not restrict auth
files or prevent a shell startup file from exporting variables again. Start a
fresh worker process to apply the policy to an already-running backend.

Launches also remove the parent's native conversation markers before the child
harness supplies its own. Resource controller identity is captured first and
retained separately, so a worker's resource requests still belong to its root.
Existing workers need a fresh backend launch for that cleanup. The native send
guard applies immediately to workers using the updated CLI/import API, including
those with inherited root markers. It enforces the supported tool contract, not
an operating-system security boundary.

## Restore and root access

Install the editable uv tool as above, then run `./install.sh --apply links` from
the repository root to link its shared skill into each harness. The mapping of
skills and instructions is in [agents](../agents/README.md).

Allow the root to execute the bridge CLI outside its sandbox, read the shared
skill and read/write the jobs directory through its harness's permission controls.
Keep the resulting grants in live machine-local files, outside this public
repository. Follow `agent-bridge guide workflow` for the workflow and `agent-bridge start --help` for backend notes.
Workers carry `AGENT_BRIDGE_WORKER`, which blocks job launches, so root
access does not grant workers permission to start more jobs. Worker sandboxing
remains in place.

## Model references

Shared model selection and reference maintenance belong to [agent-models](../agent-models/README.md).
Use `model-guide read models` and `model-guide read maintenance`; Bridge consumes their reviewed
reference without owning the refresh process. The delegation skill owns common worker coordination.

## Protocol and workflow checks

`uv run --locked pytest` covers native routing, lifecycle and recovery. The
[stream replays](tests/fixtures/README.md) exercise raw Codex JSON-RPC and fragmented
OpenCode output through production readers, alongside the existing adapter tests.
Unrelated notifications and partial frames cannot restart the RPC deadline.
An interrupt acknowledgement, a model step, a completed turn, a worker result and
the root's finished task are separate milestones. Late child completion and
failed parent notification must preserve the pending incident until its owning
delivery path can report it; they never manufacture user approval.
The [opt-in decision eval](../tests/README.md#opt-in-agent-decisions) separately
checks a model's use of the maintained guides, without adding model calls to CI.

Diagnose the exact native executable, version and execution context first.
Inventory and transport checks do not authorize a new model turn, login or plan
change. Bridge does not own harness updates: use the native installer after
identifying a version mismatch, and verify the adapter again. The desktop tool's
pinned installer remains with [computer-use](../computer-use/README.md).

## Lifecycle, delivery and privacy ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 Online --> Hidden: native connection disappears Hidden --> Online: same root reconnects ``` Discovery refreshes every ten seconds without creating per-session registrations. Native history is never archived or deleted. A selected offline root keeps its draft and receipt and never silently redirects a reply. Codex can retain a loaded root after its terminal disconnects. Claude lists only live processes; OpenCode also lists unarchived saved roots. Idle is not treated as closed. For Codex, OpenCode and ACP, transient discovery timeouts retain previously seen roots with unknown status and a connection warning. An authoritative empty list still removes them. Reading failures retain the visible transcript and disable input. They also clear the live Working indicator until native activity can be read again. An offline root invalidates pending question reads and disables its old controls; reconnection requires a fresh native pending list before answering. Suspending the page also disables input until a fresh read succeeds on return. Late reads from an earlier visit or before suspension cannot replace the current conversation or re-enable its composer. Drafts remain in tab memory throughout. | Receipt | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Queued | Native API admitted the input; the agent may not have consumed it | | Steered | Native API admitted input for steering; consumption is not confirmed | | Forwarded | Claude channel write completed; no consumption acknowledgement | | Completed | ACP returned a native prompt stop reason; its turn has ended | | Applied | Native API accepted the operation, or Inbox resolved its owned SDK question callback | | Already answered | A recorded answer already claimed this native request; no new delivery | | No longer pending | The native request was withdrawn or expired; no answer delivered | | Unknown | Dispatch may have happened; check the native chat before sending anew | These are separate milestones: recording intent, admitting a native operation, ending its turn, and finishing the user's task. A Codex stop acknowledgement means its interrupt request was accepted; the terminal `turn/completed` event establishes that the turn ended. A child result can arrive after its parent's current turn, and does not establish that the parent task is complete. For ACP answers, Applied records callback resolution; it does not acknowledge receipt or consumption by the agent. Delivery checks reuse the same request ID and payload. Unknown outcomes are never automatically resent, including after restart. Chat, commands and answers have separate receipt identities. Drafts, images and retry IDs live in tab memory: they survive root switching, but reloading discards them. `/api/send`, `/api/command` and `/api/answer` require a client UUID (`id`). Forms and permissions both use the answer route with their request handle (`form`). ACP handles bind to one exact SDK callback; OpenCode IDs come from its pending list. Optional `cancel: true` cancels a question; `decline: true` is available only when the native form advertises that action. These actions require an empty answer and cannot be combined. The receipt is persisted before dispatch: **Sending** means intent recorded, not native acceptance. Retries return its recorded outcome without redispatch. Answer receipts also claim the root/request pair transactionally, so another browser's new UUID cannot answer or cancel the same request twice. Concurrent receipt checks follow the original answer's eventual result, including Unknown. Pre-upgrade answers acquire this request claim on an exact replay; their old content hashes cannot reveal native request IDs without that replay. OpenCode owns pending forms/permissions across Inbox restarts: Inbox re-reads its native pending list before answering and rechecks a raced withdrawal after a native conflict. There is no cached pending flag to hang after restart. The capability `approvals_survive_restart` refers to an **Inbox** restart; it does not promise a provider survives its own restart. Codex blocking questions/approvals stay with their owning client, ACP callbacks expire when their SDK connection closes, and Claude's held hook ends when its process exits. In-flight receipts recover as Unknown, never as fresh work. Choices always carry native values; labels need not be unique. Question cards use the selected adapter's native question metadata, pending-request API or owned SDK callbacks. Fetch failure or page suspension preserves typed answers but disables new decisions until a fresh native list arrives. A withdrawn request or a lost acknowledgement does not authorize a second answer. Transcript text, screen scraping and keyboard simulation never create pending requests or resolve native callbacks. Question polling is independent of transcript reads, so a history failure cannot hide a newly pending native request. Inbox attaches to existing Claude terminal sessions; it does not own their SDK process or `canUseTool` callbacks and cannot retain those pending callbacks. OpenCode's existing-session form/permission API supports remote answers here. Inbox owns its ACP connection and retains the genuine SDK callback until the user answers or the connection/turn is cancelled. Native callback replay tests cover all three actions, turn cancellation, connection shutdown and durable answer receipts without a live model call. Codex async `agentMessage` items expose `questions` and `delivery=async` through `thread/items/list`. Inbox projects those exact fields. The native send API carries the question and answer as plain text, steering an active turn. Dismiss resolves the Inbox card locally. Confirmed receipts persist across restarts; native answer envelopes also resolve individual answered fields. There is no invented XML reply or attempt to answer another client's blocking callback. Ordinary later chat or image input supersedes older message-mode cards. Replaying history after a restart applies the same rule; this retires a card without inventing an answer. Claude uses its documented [PreToolUse answer contract](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#tools-that-require-user-interaction) for new questions. The hook owns the pending call, verifies session/profile/question IDs, and returns native input only after the paired user answers. Its private socket disappears when the callback ends. Already-open prompts and general tool approvals remain native. These paths do not establish shared terminal question ownership across all harnesses. OpenCode's native form IDs support answers from another client and disappear from Inbox on the next pending-list read. Codex's async cards send ordinary message input; they do not resolve another client's blocking callback. ACP requests belong to Inbox's own connection, not an existing `agy` terminal. OpenCode also reads native descendant forms and permissions through their own session routes. Child discovery allows up to 64 descendants and 200 child questions. Its soft eight-second budget is checked between children; each native HTTP operation has its own eight-second socket timeout, so a stalled read can take longer overall. Discovery failure leaves root questions available with a warning. Codex currently polls root questions only. A native child that reports `canAcceptDirectInput=false` cannot receive the adapter's ordinary message replies. Claude shares one held hook per session, including hooks from its native children. State: `${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}/agent-inbox`, configurable with `--state` or `AGENT_INBOX_HOME`. Directory mode 0700, database mode 0600. Credentials are hashed; receipts store content hashes, not text. HTTP bodies, URLs and native diagnostic contents are not logged. Approvals and secrets remain native or use [Baton](../agent-baton/README.md).
Buffers and size bounds Uploads create no directory. Preview bytes use a bounded, authenticated 32 MiB memory cache. Claude channels retain unseen attachments until read and reject new input when full. Claude reads are bounded per record (16 MiB), metadata index (32 MiB / 100,000 entries), page (100 rows, up to three pages for a tool-heavy initial view), and private helper response (24 MiB). The whole transcript has no 16 MiB cutoff. Unavailable or oversized content stays native. Channel buffers are in memory: restarting Claude loses attachments it has not read yet; images already returned by its image tool remain in native history.

This is a regression workload, not a global transcript cap or a measurement of every real session. The separate [opt-in agent decisions](../tests/README.md#opt-in-agent-decisions) evaluate how a model uses the maintained instructions; unit tests do not measure model quality. Connection diagnosis stays read-only: check the exact executable/protocol version, selected root and configured transport in their native context. Registration does not log in, update a provider or create a test conversation. An adapter mismatch should name that boundary before any authorized live-turn test. # agent-lab

[← Packages](../README.md#packages) · **uv tool + live skill and timer** · Linux / WSL

Persistent experiments for any harness or language. Ordinary files stay outside
projects and survive terminal restarts; creator and latest-run provenance stay
with them. Project changes still belong in their repository or a Git worktree.

![A lab moves from active to kept or retired; restore preserves its files, and expired retirement passes guarded cleanup before deletion.](../docs/images/agent-lab.gif)

## Use

```sh
uv tool install --editable ./agent-lab
lab=$(agent-lab new image-probe --purpose 'Compare image decoders')
agent-lab path "$lab"                       # work/ for native file/edit tools
agent-lab run "$lab" -- node --version      # any executable; exact argv, no implicit shell
agent-lab show "$lab"                       # provenance, paths, sizes and warnings
agent-lab retire "$lab" --summary 'Useful finding moved to the project docs'
agent-lab gc                               # preview; retirement grace defaults to 14 days
```

`keep ID` protects indefinitely. `restore ID` clears keep/retirement and reuses
the same paths. Repeating `retire` preserves the existing deadline. `list --sizes`
scans usage across labs; `new --json`, `list --json` and `show` support automation.
`run ID [provenance flags] -- COMMAND ...` preserves input/output and exit status.

## Files and provenance

```text
${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}/agent-lab/   private, local, outside Git
├── records/<id>.json                       purpose, creator, latest run, retirement
├── locks/                                  command leases and registry lock
└── workspaces/<id>/
    ├── work/                               command working directory
    ├── artifacts/                          outputs and evidence
    └── tmp/                                scratch that survives restarts
```

`run` exposes `AGENT_LAB_ID`, `AGENT_LAB_WORKSPACE`, `AGENT_LAB_ARTIFACTS` and
`AGENT_LAB_TMP`; its child gets `TMPDIR=tmp/`. This changes no global environment.
It also carries `AGENT_LAB_HOME`, an absolute registry override, so nested tools
keep the same lab when a harness changes `HOME` or its XDG profile. Independent
workers can receive that override when intentionally sharing labs; native sandbox
permissions still apply. `show`, `list` and `path` need read access only.
Bridge carries the host registry into its isolated worker profiles automatically.
Files are ordinary local files, not a sandbox, secret store or backup.

Provenance includes the originating directory and available Git root/branch/commit,
harness, session, model and effort. Creator and latest runner remain separate.
Detection uses the calling Codex thread's native state, Claude's exact session
and latest assistant model, OpenCode's native shell session ID, Antigravity's exported conversation ID, or Bridge's
own worker record across all four harnesses.
It never picks a nearby session or a global default. Explicit `--harness`,
`--session`, `--model`, `--effort` or corresponding `AGENT_LAB_*` variables are
optional overrides/fallbacks. Unexposed values stay null; native schema changes
do not block experiments. No account credentials,
environment dumps, command arguments or output transcripts are recorded.

After a run, and in size reports, soft warnings flag a lab at **1 GiB** or a file
at **256 MiB**. Counts are logical file sizes, exclude symlink targets and can
count hard links twice. They are warnings, not disk quotas or automatic deletion.

## Retirement and cleanup

Only registered, explicitly retired labs past their grace period qualify.
Active/kept labs, command leases, invalid metadata, redirected roots, mounts and
folders containing `.git` prevent cleanup. Git checkouts/worktrees need their
native cleanup first. Unknown folders are left alone; inspection failures never
grant permission to delete. File symlinks are removed without following targets.

Use `run` for commands that need a cleanup lease; native edits do not hold one.
Keep a lab if independent processes or manual work still need it. A wrapper
crash leaves a live direct child's inherited lease in place; an interrupted run
record with no lease indicates an unfinished receipt, not proof of a live process.
Retirement is recoverable with `restore` until GC; applied deletion is permanent.
Promote durable findings to maintained project docs before retiring experiments.

The [weekly user timer](../systemd/README.md) runs `gc --apply` through these same
checks. It never retires active labs or changes native harness histories. Install
with `./install.sh --apply links systemd`; disable with
`systemctl --user disable --now agent-lab-gc.timer`. WSL must be running for timers.

## Checks

```sh
uv sync --locked
uv run --locked pytest
uv run --locked ruff check src tests
uv run --locked ruff format --check src tests
uv run --locked ty check src
```

Native routes, task evidence and published allowances have one owner, independent
of worker orchestration. The selecting agent weighs the actual task and current
session against these observations; no model-role table or score chooses for it.
Arena, Artificial Analysis, LiveBench and Vals measure different outcomes.

The daily `agent-models-reference.timer` checks drift and conditionally polls due
sources (36h, with backoff); changed observations update the cache and generate a
numeric guide proposal when none is waiting.
No agent or Bridge is launched. Subscription facts and source contracts are
source-reviewed on demand with `refresh --record --yes`. Cached numeric observations
are usable without a human stamp per decision; no proposal applies automatically.
Pending guide review freezes that proposal while due/backoff-aware observation
polling continues; queries use the current cache, and apply reviews its saved snapshot.
Official subscription policy has a separate seven-day cache, refreshed when due
by `policy` or routine polling. It stores complete source text, digest and check
dates; a failed check retains last-good text and reports the error. `suggest`
retrieves relevant sections, tables and their qualifications from that cache;
selection never waits for a policy fetch. Missing/stale sources link to `policy`.
Text shows one policy status/drill-down per harness. Retrieved sections and their
conditions stay complete in JSON; ordinary comparisons omit unrelated policy prose.
The selecting agent interprets current conditions, exceptions and quota
opportunity cost; no plan-to-window/model/multiplier table is encoded in selection.
State belongs to `$AGENT_MODELS_HOME` or
`${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}/agent-models`; documents and review hashes live
in `src/agent_models/guide/`. Reference edits remain uncommitted.

`usage` summarizes unambiguously paired Bridge turns by the model, account and
effort requested at turn start. It does not infer the actual model or account,
task quality, quota consumption or token cost. Native effort observations are
shown separately when available. Claude token totals cover the main agent's
per-turn reported input and output, excluding cached input and helper calls;
`token_turns` shows how many turns supplied those numbers. Older and overlapping turns that
cannot be paired are counted as skipped. The source logs and conversation
content stay local.

Benchmark search returns bounded source evidence: release/retrieval dates, domain
scores, effort, available cost/time and automatically read local account hints.
Missing measurements stay unknown. The full local snapshot supports rechecks
without loading an entire leaderboard into the agent's context.

`--task` keeps the full description and combines lexical cues with local semantic
suggestions to prioritize evidence. The suggestions are not filters: task queries
retain evidence from all areas in `--json` and `--choice`, so an incomplete inference
does not hide it. With no cached model, lexical matches work without downloading;
otherwise the first semantic-only use downloads a pinned 22 MiB public embedding
model and tokenizer. Task text never leaves the machine. Use repeated `--domain`
flags to restrict evidence when needed. A task is optional for general lookup.
Without `--backend`, native
inventories are discovered independently across all four harnesses; partial
failures remain visible. No provider model is prompted. Native catalogs are read
fresh, evidence is indexed once per query, and account state is captured once.

Use optional ephemeral `--context PATH|-` JSON for actual caller restrictions and
considerations (full schema in `suggest --help`). `allowed_backends` is closed when
supplied. `allowed_routes` restricts only its listed backends using exact native
routes/aliases; omitted backends have unknown entitlement. `allowed_efforts`
intersects native controls. Account, task, session and priority descriptions stay
context for the selecting agent. Plan names, urgency, scarcity and free billing
never imply access, adequacy or a winner. Context is not persisted.

`model-guide preferences add --source user|agent --note '...'` records a private
selection note; `--backend`, `--model`, `--account`, `--task`, `--reason` and
`--expires YYYY-MM-DD` add scope and context. `preferences remove ID` deletes
one. Unexpired notes appear in `suggest` with user-attributed notes first. Source
is caller attribution, not an identity check. Notes inform judgment; they do not
prove entitlement, restrict routes, or replace explicit task context.

Every admitted route and supported measured effort remains in `--json`, including
unmeasured models and missing speed. The default comparison shows up to 12 models:
the current session, distinct access/billing pools and source-scoped examples of
quality, cost, time and intermediate tradeoffs. Equivalent underlying models share
a comparison while their execution/billing routes stay distinct. Each example
shows selected measured efforts with their paired score, cost and time, preserving
missing prices and source/run scope. Inclusion reasons describe the evidence or
route shown; they do not recommend a winner. Native effort choices and account
windows are shown separately; a window is attached to a route only when its
native observation names that exact model. Different sample counts stay visible. Speed
points keep effort, tokens/s, first-token latency and workload together; the brief includes
a measured middle native effort when available as well as speed extremes. These are
source measurements, not predictions of this job's cost or duration.
Inspect `--choice ROUTE` for other settings and run scope;
use flexible `--query` discovery or `--limit N --offset K` to page the comparison
(JSON pages native inventory order). There is no winner shortlist, tier/newness bonus, combined
score or cheapest-first policy. Native aliases share a resolved model, while
OpenCode provider/free variants remain separate execution routes.

`--choice EXACT_NATIVE_ROUTE --effort LEVEL` preserves explicit choices and reports
problems without substitution. Measurements at other efforts are shown separately,
not treated as results at the selected effort. Optional `--max-usd`/`--max-seconds` constrain each
published source observation; unknowns cannot establish a bound or prove actual
route spend/latency. Reviewed model links transfer model evidence, not provider
reliability, speed, price or entitlement. Account overrides are supported only by
agy's native listing; other backends use their selected native session.

Source/version, dates, samples, intervals, harness, configuration and workload
remain available in JSON. Task duration, response/first-token latency and tokens/s
are distinct. Legacy cached AA speed and model release dates are recovered in
memory without fetch or proposal approval; reported zero remains validity-unknown.
Native descriptions/modalities are facts or claims, not task-quality scores.
Vision perception and browser/OSWorld outcomes remain separate.

Queries show **quality leaders** and **cost-efficient choices** as separate bounded
views, so a small limit does not hide cheap workers. Frontiers are recalculated
after native/query filtering, within the same source, release and metric; table
runs with different harnesses stay separate. API cost is not subscription quota.
`--domain backend` uses coding and terminal evidence and names the gaps in database,
security and service-architecture coverage. Writing retains its text-preference
scope. `--brief` keeps source dates, confidence intervals, run settings and account
freshness in compact text; omit it for JSON and the complete returned fields.

`--backend` matches exact model identities from Codex, Claude, Antigravity or
OpenCode; `--query` narrows by native ID/alias. Claude aliases resolve through
initialization with no prompt, session history, hooks or MCP launches. Codex and
Claude publish per-model effort metadata; OpenCode's native API CLI supplies
enabled models and variants for the current directory. agy's text listing leaves
efforts unknown: verify its selected native controls. `--account` scopes cached
account observations; only agy supports an explicit native inventory account.
Otherwise the listing uses the current native profile. No account is switched.
Native responses are captured through a temporary regular-file handle: OpenCode
can truncate large JSON when it exits while pipe output is still pending. The
file closes after each read; catalogs and account observations are not tracked.

Use a model/effort exposed by the actual native worker tool. The selecting agent
weighs task fit, verification, context/setup, allowance and risk; benchmark values
cannot establish these task-specific costs. Bridge owns cross-harness execution.

Listings describe native CLI inventory, not entitlement or the models selectable
by a particular native subagent tool. Account caches are separate observations;
the current session's native controls remain authoritative. The reviewed OpenCode
privacy allowlist lives in inventory.py and is also consumed by Bridge.

OpenCode's listing marks named free variants; `unverified` means the catalog does
not establish billing for other IDs. It does not mean paid, unavailable or out
of included quota. Preserve the requested provider/model/variant, and verify a
chat request in the matching native CLI/session. A service catalog or API error
does not establish the result for a standalone CLI session.

Shared orchestration does not own provider protocols or account lifecycle.

# agent-resources

[← Packages](../README.md#packages) · **uv tool** · host resource admission

![Heavy commands declare their needs to a shared queue. Native agent or Bridge job IDs label wrapped commands; Wake and Bridge show their reservations and available command memory readings. Exit releases the reservation.](../docs/images/agent-resources.gif)

Cooperative admission for memory-heavy or sustained multi-core commands. Kernel
locks hold reservations across exec and release them on process exit. This is
resource coordination, not a sandbox.

```sh
uv tool install --editable ./agent-resources
agent-resources run --mem 2G -- uv run pytest
agent-resources run --mem 3G --exclusive -- ./benchmark
agent-resources list
agent-resources list --json --owner claude:SESSION_ID
agent-resources guide
```

Arguments, environment, stdin, signals and exit status pass through. Bridge
filters its worker environment before launch; this runner does not strip secrets
from an ordinary command. Jobs can run concurrently when their declared needs
fit. Reserve exclusivity for measurements, not test suites. Never detach the
command; detached descendants are outside the lease's guarantee. Agents start
long or queued runs as a native harness background job so steers still arrive
([guide](src/agent_resources/guide.md)).

`list` explains queued requests with their admission reason, memory need versus
free/budget, queue position and number of requests behind them. It reuses the
admission policy against current readings; redirected command output is not
needed to diagnose a wait.

Use `list --json --owner <controller>` for a versioned snapshot with
`agent_id`, declared need and queue state. For native agent attribution, pass
`--agent-id ID` to `run` or set `AGENT_RESOURCES_AGENT_ID` on that wrapped local
command. This labels the command reservation; it is not an agent memory reading
or cap.

The private queue is `/tmp/agent-resources-<uid>` or `$AGENT_RESOURCES_HOME`,
independent of HOME/TMPDIR. All participants on a host use the same queue path.
`AGENT_RESOURCES_SLICE` names an optional shared systemd budget (default agent.slice);
Bridge supplies its existing codex.slice integration explicitly. Worker environments
carry a controller identity and cannot mutate the queue or list other owners' requests;
they can read JSON rows filtered to that exact controller. The snapshot's admission
totals remain shared across the host. Cancellation of a known
controller's request requires that exact root identity. This protects against
accidental session crossover, not an untrusted process with the same OS account.

An explicit memory cap must be enforceable; an unavailable systemd scope is an
error. Existing inherited caps are preserved. Inspect actual limits and use
real-workload peak measurements when choosing a memory estimate.

Checks (from this directory):

```sh
uv sync --locked
uv run --locked pytest
uv run --locked ruff check src tests
```

See `agent-resources guide`
for admission policy, inherited limits, cancellation and its sources.

# agent-session

[← Packages](../README.md#packages) · **Library** (editable dependency, no CLI)

One answer to "which conversation is calling?", shared by Bridge, Baton, Resources and Lab.

```python
import agent_session

agent_session.native()  # ("claude", "<session id>"), ("codex", …), ("agy", …), ("opencode", …), or None
```

A process can inherit an enclosing session's variables: Claude Code started from a Codex
terminal still sees `CODEX_THREAD_ID`. The running harness's own marker therefore wins:

| Order | Harness | Variables |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Claude Code | `CLAUDECODE=1`, `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` (the session is `None` when Claude hides it) |
| 2 | Antigravity | `ANTIGRAVITY_CONVERSATION_ID` |
| 3 | OpenCode | `OPENCODE=1`, `OPENCODE_SESSION_ID` (native shell tools in 2.2.6) |
| 4 | Codex | `CODEX_THREAD_ID` |
| 5 | Declared | `AGENT_BRIDGE_ROOT_HARNESS`, `AGENT_BRIDGE_ROOT_SESSION` |

A bare `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` without `CLAUDECODE` is an inherited ID, not a Claude
session. Empty means unknown; whitespace, control characters or more than 200 characters
raise `ValueError` instead of falling through to another identity.
`environment(harness, session)` is the inverse, for tools that launch a child as a given
session; `VARIABLES` lists everything to drop first.

OpenCode's [versioned shell implementation](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v2.2.6/packages/core/src/tool/plugin/shell.ts)
sets its marker and exact session ID together. A bare inherited `OPENCODE_SESSION_ID`
does not identify the caller. Model and effort remain unknown when the native
runtime does not expose them; no global context file is inferred.

Tool-specific policy stays with each tool: Baton's `AGENT_BATON_SESSION`, Resources'
`AGENT_RESOURCES_OWNER`, a Bridge worker's own job, Lab's `/proc` lookup when Claude hides
its ID, and each tool's stored identity format.
Codex's [root-session environment](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.166.0/codex-rs/core/src/exec_env.rs)
also supplies `CODEX_SESSION_ID`. Resources uses it to group native child commands under
their root controller; `native()` still identifies the child's own `CODEX_THREAD_ID`.
`VARIABLES` includes both IDs so independent launches discard the enclosing session.

Installed through its consumers (`install.sh` passes `--with-editable`). Checks:

```sh
uv sync --locked
uv run --locked pytest
uv run --locked ruff check src tests
```

# agents

[← Packages](../README.md#packages) · **Live** · `./install.sh --apply links`

Shared guidance and task skills for Codex, Claude Code, Antigravity and OpenCode.
The [repository placement policy](../AGENTS.md#guidance-placement) governs changes:
keep enough context to choose and execute correctly, with one owner for details.

[Host feedback workflow and public templates](feedback/README.md) support private
local issues and comments. Only agents working on dotfiles review that queue;
the shared global guidance asks other agents to report relevant tooling friction.

## Instruction and skill map

| Scope | Maintained source | Live discovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared globals | `.config/agents/AGENTS.md` | All four harnesses |
| Codex globals | [codex/.codex/AGENTS.md](../codex/.codex/AGENTS.md) | `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`; reads shared globals, then Codex preferences |
| Claude globals | [claude/.claude/CLAUDE.md](../claude/.claude/CLAUDE.md) | `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`; imports shared globals and adds Claude preferences |
| Antigravity globals | [gemini/.gemini/AGENTS.md](../gemini/.gemini/AGENTS.md) | `~/.gemini/AGENTS.md`; includes shared globals, then agy preferences |
| OpenCode globals | [opencode/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md](../opencode/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md) | `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`; combined with shared globals by `opencode.jsonc` |
| Shared skills | `.agents/skills/` | Codex/OpenCode: `~/.agents/skills`; Claude: `~/.claude/skills`; agy: `~/.gemini/config/skills` |
| Codex-only skills | [codex/.codex/skills/](../codex/.codex/skills/) | `~/.codex/skills`; includes `codex-wake` |

Each harness owns an appendable global file. Claude and Antigravity import the
shared source; OpenCode loads it through its native `instructions` config.
Codex explicitly reads it because its global instruction loader has no documented
include directive. Append only harness-wide preferences; project invariants stay
in project instructions.

Skill names/descriptions provide discovery; the body supplies the workflow.
Keep the first action and non-obvious constraints there. Load references only for
the selected mode, and use CLI help for changing flags/defaults. Prefer an
enforced contract or native tool behavior when it can replace a remembered rule.

## Shared tools

- `model-selection`: model/effort choices for main sessions or workers, backed by
  `model-guide` and its independently maintained references.
- `delegation`: shared worker planning and verification, with native harness
  references loaded only when needed. Bridge is its cross-harness execution route.
- `agent-bridge`: root coordination across harnesses. Its skill routes to
  `agent-bridge guide workflow`, which owns launch/watch/group/cleanup behavior.
  Backend notes and CLI discovery own available models and flags.
- `agent-baton`: secret handoffs and unanswered-question reminders. Its skill
  retains secret handling, conversation isolation and target-focus constraints;
  `agent-baton --help` owns forms and command schemas.
- `python-project`: the substantial Python baseline, including uv, type checking,
  quality tools and CI. Small scripts and narrow fixes keep proportional scope.
- `agent-lab`: persistent experiments outside repositories, with creator/latest-run
  provenance, size warnings and retirement. Its CLI owns layout and cleanup checks.
- `resource-admission`: heavy foreground work from any harness, using the independent
  agent-resources queue rather than requiring Bridge orchestration.
- `agent-desktop`: Windows native GUI work from WSL through a Baton-guarded launcher;
  loads installed upstream guides and owns desktop session cleanup. Setup and limits:
  [computer-use](../computer-use/README.md).

The global rules retain authorization, question escalation, ownership,
verification and boundary safety. Detailed language-specific workflows belong
to their skills. Harness-specific cache notes live in
[Codex](../codex/README.md#cache-and-resuming-threads),
[Claude](../claude/README.md#cache-and-thread-reuse) and
[Antigravity](../gemini/README.md#cache-and-thread-reuse).

## Engineering skills

Nine [pstack](https://github.com/backnotprop/pstack) skills are based on commit
[`fad8d01588a1`](https://github.com/backnotprop/pstack/tree/fad8d01588a1b1ae803f87c8a1e0de79e28cffec),
with their references and [MIT license](PSTACK-LICENSE). They are locally adapted:
native tools/model discovery replace Cursor-specific calls and guessed model
slugs; absent companion skills are not required; searches and delegation fit the
task; commits/publication retain the user's authorization boundary.

| Use | Skills |
| --- | --- |
| Prevent recurring repository mistakes | `correct` |
| Validate measured performance claims | `benchmark-checklist` |
| Create or audit app verification workflows | `create-verification-skill`, `maintain-verification-skill` |
| Explain execution or historical rationale | `how`, `why` |
| Assess risk beyond a diff | `blast-radius` |
| Compare requested candidates or edit prose | `arena`, `unslop` |

Automatic matching is enabled; descriptions narrow when a workflow is relevant.
A skill's availability does not authorize extra agents, product edits or external
actions. The full upstream plugin is not required or installed. To refresh the
vendored skills, review upstream against the pinned baseline, preserve local
scope/portability adaptations and license, then update the attribution.

Manual recovery backups remain outside Git under
`${XDG_STATE_HOME:-$HOME/.local/state}/backups/<scope>/<timestamp>/`, with private
permissions and original paths/restore details. Application-managed backups stay
in their own locations.
