agent-baton hands a question or secret prompt to the human on their phone or PC.
Ordinary answers are returned to the agent; secrets stay private and are typed into an approved app.
Never put secrets in a question or chat.

Native tools: `agent-baton mcp` serves MCP over stdio. Register with
`codex mcp add agent_baton -- agent-baton mcp`, then reload the harness.
Every call supplies its conversation owner, matching the CLI's session namespace;
the package README lists tools and isolation. Secret values are never inputs or
results. CLI commands below remain available for every workflow.

Pick the command
  question  ordinary text or multiple-choice question; wait returns the answer as JSON.
  form   one-off ordinary form from a JSON file; wait returns answers keyed by question id.
  ask    any login or secret you must enter in a browser or app (the usual case).
  env    have the human store a secret in one or more environment files.
  run    a command that needs a password: sudo, ssh passphrase, gpg, git credential prompt.
  pass   only when the human must do the sign-in themselves on the PC (CAPTCHA, passkey, QR).
         Browser and screen tools are blocked until they hand it back.

Session isolation
  Codex (CODEX_THREAD_ID), Claude Code (CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID), Antigravity
  (ANTIGRAVITY_CONVERSATION_ID) and OpenCode 2.2.2 (OPENCODE_SESSION_ID) are identified automatically. Other
  harnesses must supply AGENT_BATON_SESSION with a unique, nonsecret conversation id on every call
  (create one once, then reuse it in this conversation); an explicit value overrides the automatic one.
  Example: AGENT_BATON_SESSION=conversation-UUID agent-baton question "Which scope?"
  Use the same value for wait, withdraw, type, forget and status. Never set a shared value in shell startup.
  AGENT_BATON_BY changes the display name only; it does not isolate sessions.
  Default selection and explicit ids/sites are limited to your session. Without an owner, state commands
  fail closed; old requests without an owner are never adopted. Human pages remain tied to their request.
  Two simultaneous questions have separate notification tags and one-use reply links. Answering one
  does not answer, consume or withdraw the other. Multiple open requests in one session require an id.
  The shared browser/screen lock during a human login is global for privacy; questions never take it.

Ordinary questions (root/coordinator only)
  Use your harness's native question tool first, preferring its nonblocking variant (chat if unavailable).
  If the root is able to keep working and the question is still
  pending after the delay in your shared instructions, send one reminder with the same wording/options:
  agent-baton question "Which scope?" --option "Current project" --option "All projects"
  Omit --option for free text. Choices always include Other with a text box; none is selected for them.
  Yes/no or approval questions use explicit --option "Yes, proceed" --option "No" choices.
  Add --multiple for select-all-that-apply; answer is always a JSON list in option order, with Other last.
  Without --multiple, answer is one string. Each invocation collects one question.
  agent-baton wait <id> --until-done      (as a background command: it ends when the human answers or it expires)
  An answered question returns JSON with id, question and answer. A foreground call needs
  --timeout N instead; exit 75 then means still held.
  No browser tools are blocked and no typing happens. Answers are readable by the agent and stored
  locally (0600); resolved state is cleaned on a later launch after about a day. Never use this for secrets.
  If the human answers in the harness first: agent-baton withdraw <id>
  Withdrawal only closes an ordinary question and never approves anything. Workers send questions
  to their root instead of notifying the human. Silence, expiry and cancellation are not consent.
  A question form does not replace mandatory harness permission/approval dialogs.
  This CLI does not monitor harness questions or start a reminder timer; the active root does that.
  For blocking native questions, prefer the harness's supported remote-answer/notification path.
  Do not simulate keys or fabricate answers to dismiss the prompt. Native hooks have no portable
  cancel-after-delay operation; see the README's Native questions and hooks section.

One-off forms (the same root-only reminder policy applies)
  agent-baton form /tmp/decision.json
  JSON shape:
    {"title":"Review choices","questions":[
      {"id":"scope","question":"Scope?","type":"choice","options":["Local","Shared"]},
      {"id":"platforms","question":"Platforms?","type":"multiple","options":["Linux","Windows"]},
      {"id":"notes","question":"Other constraints?","type":"text","required":false}
    ]}
  Types: text (multiline), choice, multiple. required defaults to true; unanswered optional fields
  are omitted from the returned answers object. --ttl controls expiry; withdraw also works on forms.
  wait returns {"id":"...","title":"...","answers":{"scope":"Local","platforms":["Linux"]}}.
  Bounds: definition 64 KiB; title 120 characters; optional top-level reason 300; 1–10 questions;
  unique lowercase ids up to 32 characters; question 2000; at most 10 options of 300 each; answer 2000.
  Unknown keys, duplicate JSON keys, non-finite values, invalid types and ambiguous submissions fail.
  This is a CLI JSON interface, not a public HTTP API. Forms use built-in controls, never arbitrary
  agent-supplied HTML or scripts. Do not use this interface for credentials.

Logins with ask + type
  1. Look at the page with your own tools to see what it wants (email, password, code).
  2. `agent-baton windows` lists window titles. Pick a distinctive part of the title of the
     window the field is in, e.g. "Sign in" or "Google Accounts". It may not be a terminal.
     Titles often change between steps (Google: "Sign in", then "Welcome"): repeat --window
     for each title you expect, because the human approves exactly those.
  3. agent-baton ask --window "<title part>" --reason "<why>" email="Account email" password:secret=Password
     Each field is name[:secret]=Label. `:secret` shows as a password input. The human sees the
     fields, your reason and the window title, then answers on a form.
  4. `agent-baton wait <id> --until-done` in the background, and do other work meanwhile.
  5. `agent-baton focus --id <id>` activates the approved window. Then click its field with your own tool
     and `agent-baton type <name> --id <id>` (`--clear` replaces existing text). Extension browser actions
     can work in background tabs; select the intended tab for this desktop typing step. Windows typing
     refuses a background window instead of stealing field focus. Check that the masked field filled
     before submitting (`--enter` submits immediately). Never read a password value back.
  6. `agent-baton forget <id>` after confirming submission succeeded. Answers also expire on their own
     (default 10 minutes).

Store a human-supplied environment secret
  agent-baton env LIQUID_API_KEY --prefix liquid_ --file ~/.config/shell/secrets.local.sh --file .env --reason "Configure the API client"
  The human gets a masked field with the variable name, target files and reason. The value is stored
  by the daemon and never returned to the agent. Existing entries are replaced; `.sh` files get
  `export`, other files get plain `NAME=value`. Existing targets are backed up under
  `$XDG_STATE_HOME/backups/env-secrets/` (or `~/.local/state/backups/env-secrets/`); the backup's
  `origin.json` records restore paths. Targets and backups are mode 0600; symlinks and group/world
  writable targets are refused. Prefix and value must contain only letters, numbers, `_`, `.`, `-`.
  `wait <id>` reports the paths and backup location, never the value. Cancellation or expiry writes nothing.

Commands that need a password
  agent-baton run --reason "<why>" -- sudo apt-get install -y foo
  The human reviews the exact command, presses Run and types any password on the page. Then
  `agent-baton wait <id>` returns the exit code, stdout and stderr (the prompt text stays private).

Rules
  - Never put a secret in agent-visible chat or a command line. Use `env` only when the human asked to store it in environment files.
  - `back` and `cancel` belong to the human; the guard denies them to you. Agents may withdraw only ordinary questions.
  - cancelled or expired means stop and ask the user; do not retry on your own.
  - While a `pass` baton is out, browser and desktop tools are denied. That is expected.
  - Password managers, saved passwords and chrome://settings/passwords are never to be browsed.
  - If no channel reached the human, tell them in chat. `agent-baton doctor` names what is broken.

# Host admission and pressure

Use `agent-resources run --mem SIZE -- <command>`
only for model inference/benchmarks, dataset download/extraction, full test
suites, long-lived local servers/headless browsers, or commands expected to use
more than about 1 GiB or several cores for more than a minute.
Do not wrap worker runners, git, edits, reads, lint, type checks or targeted tests.
Everything else runs directly; commands are never automatically wrapped.
Declare the expected peak with `--mem` (for example `1G` or `2500M`). Add
`--exclusive` only for timing measurements, never for test suites. Fitting jobs
run concurrently. Wrap a compound job with `agent-resources run --mem 1G -- sh -c '...'`.
Never detach the command (`&`, `nohup`, `setsid`, `disown`, self-daemonizing):
the wrapper must stay the command's own process for its whole lifetime, servers
included. Do not nest wrappers. Do not hold your turn on it either: start any run
that may queue or last more than a short wait as the harness's native background
job (a background shell or yielded terminal), keep working, and collect it through
the harness's completion notice. A blocking tool call holds back coordinator steers
until it returns.
Waiting for a slot is normal, never a blocker or progress message to send. Report
only a holder shown dead while still blocked or a wait exceeding 30 minutes,
excluding time paused by root. A root pause is normal; wait for resume.
Bridge workers report such blockers to their own root with an ordinary `URGENT:`
job message. Native `agent-bridge message send` is root-to-root only; the root
coordinates with another request's root when needed. Workers never relay sibling
traffic through root; use ordinary `TO <peer>:` job messages without native discovery.

```sh
agent-resources run --mem 1G -- uv run pytest
agent-resources run --mem 2500M --exclusive -- ./benchmark
agent-resources list
agent-resources list --json --owner claude:SESSION_ID
```

## Root queue controls

```sh
agent-resources list
agent-resources cancel <id>
agent-resources cancel <owner>/<job>
agent-resources pause --reason "reviewing host load"
agent-resources resume
```

Workers (`AGENT_RESOURCES_WORKER`) cannot list globally or change the queue; they
may read `list --json --owner <exact-controller-identity>` for that controller's
request rows. Workers may still run commands through `agent-resources run --mem SIZE -- ...`.
`list` shows each live request's id, owning job, executable basename (never arguments), declared need,
exclusivity, running/queued/cancelling state, wait/elapsed time and kernel-lock
liveness. Dead unlocked records and their control metadata are removed on scan.
`list --json` emits schema version 1; `--owner` filters its request rows by exact
controller identity while admission totals remain host-wide. `run --agent-id ID`
or `AGENT_RESOURCES_AGENT_ID=ID agent-resources run ...` labels a wrapped local
command with its native agent loop. The label does not measure or cap the model
loop; `--mem` remains an admission estimate.
Actual per-command memory use/cap is attributable only when the command has its
own readable cgroup scope. Shared or inherited cgroup readings are not
per-command measurements.
Queued rows also show position, the current admission reason, reserved/budget/free
memory and `waiting_behind` (later queued requests, including ones that may backfill).
Reasons identify an earlier selected or blocking request by ID. These are fresh
snapshots using the caller's limits/environment; inspect from the owning session
when its policy differs. A finite CPU quota needs a one-second usage sample,
outside the queue lock. Unavailable host readings leave requests visible with an
explicit diagnostic, rather than reporting readiness.
An id identifies one request, not the worker job. `cancel` also accepts an exact
`owner/job`, but refuses if that job has multiple requests; use a listed id.

Cancelling a queued request prevents admission; on its next poll (normally one
second) the waiting command prints `cancelled by root while queued; exit=125`
on stderr and exits **125**. That code is reserved for queue cancellation; normal
command exit codes still pass through and could themselves be 125. Cancelling a
running request sends **SIGTERM**, then **SIGKILL after five seconds** if still
alive. New commands have their own process group, so foreground children are
stopped too and the worker runner continues. Running commands retain their
normal signal exit status. A process that escapes its process group by
daemonizing is unsupported; keep servers attached to the wrapper.

Cancellation verifies process identity against the inherited request descriptor
and checks process start times before escalation; it never signals a worker
runner's process group. Run controls from the host root harness so `/proc`
can see holder processes. Cancellation checks controller identity before changing a request. A known controller's request
can be cancelled only from that exact root session.

`pause` admits no new heavy commands; running commands and ordinary unwrapped
work continue. The default reason is `maintenance`; reasons are at most 200
characters without control characters. Waiters print `paused by root: <reason>`
and `owners`/`watch` show the pause. Pause time is excluded from the 30-minute
wait report threshold, including waits spanning multiple pauses. Repeating pause
can update its reason without resetting its clock. Pause persists across a root
or waiter crash until explicit `agent-resources resume`; a dead process is not an implicit
resume. Private control files use atomic replacement, and orphaned per-request
files are cleaned using the kernel lock rather than PID guesses.

## Admission

The queue is shared across owners, working directories and harnesses of the same
Unix user on one Linux host. It uses `/tmp/agent-resources-<uid>` (0700), not
the job directory or a harness's HOME. OpenCode mounts this directory through its
private `/tmp`; sandbox restrictions otherwise remain in force. Other users and
machines have separate queues. `AGENT_RESOURCES_HOME` can relocate it; every
participant must use the same local filesystem directory. Do not delete it while
commands are active or waiting.

A short flock protects admission. Every request holds its own flock, inherited
across exec into the command. Each running request reserves its declared need.
Exit, SIGKILL or an OOM kill releases the lock and reservation; the next scan
discards unlocked request files without PID-based stale-lock guesses.
Command stdio, signals and exit status pass through. An application that explicitly
closes inherited descriptors can drop its lock early; keep such an application
under a shell that waits for it (`sh -c 'app'`). Detaching or daemonizing outside
the wrapper is unsupported; a native harness background job is not detaching. This is cooperative admission, not sandbox enforcement.

Each private `.request` file next to `gate.lock` records job name, executable
basename (no command arguments), start time, PID and PID namespace. Host PID is
recorded directly when known; a host-side `owners`/`watch` scan resolves a
namespaced holder and updates its record. Before that scan, or when host process
visibility is unavailable, it says `host_pid=unavailable` instead of guessing.
Cancellation can also resolve a visible holder when its recorded host namespace
is wrong, but only if its namespace, local PID and inherited request descriptor
uniquely match.
The matching `.request.need` file (0600) stores declared need, exclusivity,
queue time and optional job cap. Missing or malformed request metadata stops
admission rather than guessing a reservation.
Wait messages show queue position, every holder's job/command and declared need, elapsed time and
`alive=yes (kernel lock)`, normally every thirty seconds. Kernel lock checks work
across separate PID namespaces. Unlocked holder records are dead/stale and removed;
if admission is still blocked, the waiter reports the dead holder. No holder
record is trusted as proof of liveness without its lock.

Admission requires enough shared memory and headroom. The resource reader checks
`/proc/meminfo` (`MemAvailable`), `/proc/loadavg` (one-minute load), and the
cgroup v2 membership in `/proc/self/cgroup`. It reads `memory.current`,
`memory.max`, `memory.events`, `cpu.max` and `cpu.stat` along the inherited
hierarchy, including the worker's job scope and configured shared slice. A root
outside that slice also reads its standard user-manager path when present.
`AGENT_RESOURCES_SLICE` defaults to `agent.slice`; Bridge selects its existing
`codex.slice` explicitly for its workers.
Live shared headroom is the minimum of host `MemAvailable` and
`memory.max - memory.current` for the shared slice and its finite ancestors, minus
the safety floor. The caller's smaller job scope does not reduce this shared
headroom; that scope still enforces its cap on the command. Without a shared
slice, inherited cgroups and host readings determine the headroom. Reclaimable
cgroup cache is deliberately not counted as slack.
Missing controllers are labelled unavailable; malformed or unreadable discovered
budgets stop admission. With no cgroup v2 membership, admission uses host readings.

Admit a request only when the sum of **all running declared needs plus its need**
fits shared capacity (the tightest host total/ancestor limit) minus the safety
floor, and **its new need alone** fits live shared headroom after that floor.
Running memory is already reflected in `MemAvailable`/`memory.current` and is not
subtracted again from live free memory. Status shows `heavy_reserved` and the
capacity-based `heavy_budget`; wait messages also show live `free`. A need larger
than shared capacity minus the floor is rejected rather than waiting forever.

Omitting `--mem` reserves **1 GiB**. It matches the heavy-work threshold and
avoids charging every unannotated test suite for an entire worker scope. It is a
default estimate, not a measured peak: declare larger needs for model/data work.
Memory sizes use positive bytes or K/M/G/T binary units, including exact fractions
such as `1.5G`. This declaration neither allocates memory nor changes cgroup caps.

The oldest fitting request normally goes first. If the head does not fit, the
first smaller request that fits may backfill. After the head has waited **five
minutes**, no more jobs may backfill until it can start. Already-running jobs
continue; the five-minute bound limits new overtaking, not their runtime.
An exclusive request is also a FIFO barrier: jobs behind it cannot backfill past
it. It starts only with no other heavy jobs running and excludes all heavy
admissions until it exits. It does not stop ordinary unwrapped commands.

The first cgroup CPU sample takes one second. Admission then waits while a
limited shared ancestor uses at least 80% of its quota over the sampling interval, or
its throttled-period count increases. Host load remains a separate gate: host
load cannot reliably be attributed to a slice. No cgroups, limits or slice
drop-ins are modified by admission.

| Environment setting | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AGENT_RESOURCES_SLOTS` | Unset: no job-count cap | Optional positive hard cap in addition to memory admission. |
| `AGENT_RESOURCES_MIN_AVAILABLE_MIB` | Existing floor: larger of 1024 MiB and 20% of the smallest host/inherited memory capacity | Reserve memory before admitting more work. `0` disables the reserve. |
| `AGENT_RESOURCES_MAX_LOAD` | 80% of logical CPU count | Leave host scheduling headroom; positive finite values only. |

Set these in the root environment before launching workers so they inherit a
consistent policy. If live requests have different explicit caps, the tightest
cap applies; unset requests do not impose a count limit. Queue position,
memory needs/budget, holders and the wait reason go to stderr on change (at most every five seconds), with
a reminder every thirty seconds. Cancellation while waiting releases the request.

These reserve and CPU thresholds are conservative starting policies, not a
measured guarantee for arbitrary workloads. A single command can still exceed
its budget after admission. Confirm them with representative peak working sets,
queue times, slice OOM counters and repeated benchmark timings on the real host
before relying on declared estimates or increasing concurrency. A process can
grow beyond its declaration; kernel cgroup caps remain the final defense.
Use `--exclusive` for benchmark timing isolation. A memory estimate alone cannot
prevent CPU contention; test suites must not request exclusivity.
Light commands must run directly rather than joining this queue.

## Existing limits and optional caps

Bridge workers already inherit their job scope and slice caps. Their children
stay in those cgroups. Heavy keeps that membership: it never moves a constrained
worker into an unrelated scope to apply another cap. With `--memory-max-mib`, an
inherited cap at least as strict already satisfies the request; a request to
tighten it fails before the command runs. Changing live job or
slice limits is a separate root decision.

For an invocation without inherited memory caps or its configured shared slice, the
flag attempts a systemd user scope with `MemoryMax`. A bounded no-op probe checks
the same properties first. Absent systemd, an inaccessible user bus (including
WSL configurations), or an unsupported scope causes an error before the command runs.
The real command is never retried after a scope launch failure. On systemd
versions with argument expansion, expansion is disabled to preserve literal
arguments. No new cap is enabled by default: a safe working set cannot be guessed
for both model servers and test suites.

Bridge consumes these measurements in its own `owners`/`watch` views. Its integration
owns job attribution, OOM history and wake policy; this tool never acknowledges
agent events or resumes a conversation.

## Why this design

[GNU Parallel](https://www.gnu.org/software/parallel/man.html) combines job
counts with `--load` and `--memfree`; its memory policy can kill and requeue the
youngest job below half the threshold. This queue borrows admission gates, without
killing or replaying potentially stateful worker commands.
[GNU make `-l`](https://www.gnu.org/software/make/manual/html_node/Parallel.html)
also delays new recipes under load, but permits a first job; this queue waits even
for the first heavy job when the host or slice lacks headroom.

The [kernel cgroup v2 contract](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)
defines inherited, hierarchical limits, `memory.events` OOM counts and CPU quota
statistics. [systemd resource control](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.resource-control.html)
recommends `MemoryHigh` for normal control and `MemoryMax` as the last defense;
limits are separate from admission. [systemd-run](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd-run.html)
scope mode preserves the caller's environment and runs synchronously.
[WSL supports systemd](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/systemd),
but that does not establish user-bus availability inside a worker sandbox.

[nice](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/nice.1.html) and
[ionice](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/ionice.1.html) change scheduling
priority; they neither reserve memory nor exclude competing benchmarks. Existing
worker niceness stays in place. No additional scheduler or dependency is needed.

# agy backend (Antigravity CLI)

- Read `model-guide models --backend agy` for the models, but pass Bridge the base model and the level separately: `agy models` fuses the level into the name (`gemini-3.8-flash-low`) while an ACP session offers `gemini-3.8-flash` plus `--effort low|medium|high`, and rejects the fused name. A rejected model's error lists what the session offers; use task evidence and actual account constraints for selection. Native inventory is distinct from Bridge's existing GPT-OSS policy exclusion.
- Quota observations retain native bucket IDs, window periods, reset times and reported model membership. A provider group name, equal percentages or matching resets do not establish shared membership or model access.
- `agy-auth` owns account inventory and sign-in. A worker uses the current CLI account. Each worker receives its own private credential. Refreshed credentials return to the registry only if the original registry snapshot is unchanged.
- Bridge reads the selected thinking level from the native ACP session configuration.
- **Compact**: `agent-bridge compact <job>` resumes an idle session, discovers ACP's compact command and confirms a new native checkpoint before reporting success.
- Both modes read anywhere. workspace-write may write the cwd plus writable roots and run commands confined by agy's sandbox, with no network. read-only denies writes and commands.
  - Network or more commands are opt-in through agy's allow rules; deny beats allow.
  - A denial is logged as urgent, and the worker is told once to continue without it.
- Bridge uses AGY's [ACP steering](https://antigravity.google/docs/ide/extensions/acp/) to send a prompt during an active turn. `--queue` holds it for the next turn. The native echo confirms delivery; if the connection fails before confirmation, inspect the session before retrying. Interrupt ends the active turn. Conversation state is isolated per job and removed with the job.
- Quota out: change the current account with `agy-auth` before resuming the worker. Before that, the runner reads its own login's cached quota every two minutes and asks `agent-accounts` to refresh it (at most about every ten), then raises `quota_pressure` for a window that covers the worker's model: by AGY's reported model set when it gives one, otherwise by the group's name, since `/usage` names its groups ("Gemini Models", "Claude and GPT models") without listing models. A worker on a `gemini-*`, `claude-*` or `gpt-*` model matches a group naming that family; any other model matches nothing. The warning says when the match was inferred from a name. Readings are as coarse as the refresh.
- Waiting costs quota: agy backgrounds long commands and repeated polling can spend model requests. The runner checks the native transcript when available and raises an urgent `quota_burn` after sustained requests without streamed activity. Briefs should keep agy workers off long benchmarks; the runner tells them to hand such a command to the coordinator and end the turn.

## Quota and accounts
When a turn fails with a usage or limit error:
1. Run `codex-auth list`. The 5H/WEEKLY columns are percent remaining from local cache only, so an account idle for hours can show stale numbers. On tiers without a five-hour limit, the 5H column can repeat the weekly value. Live output may label the $100 tier differently from the pricing page. Mask emails in any output you show.
2. Switch to an authorized account with sufficient allowance by email without printing it: `codex-auth switch "$(codex-auth list | awk '$1=="NN"{print $2}')"` (a bare number doesn't match). Choose from live access and remaining windows rather than assuming a particular set of tiers.
3. Run `codex app-server daemon restart` so the new login applies; codex-auth alone doesn't.
4. Resume one failed job and confirm it progresses for ~30 s before resuming the rest. If it still fails at once, move to the next account.

Use another backend only when every account is exhausted.

# OpenCode backend

- **Models**: `model-guide models --backend opencode --json` reports the connected service's model IDs and published variants. It is inventory, not a standalone-session or entitlement check: test a non-free model with `opencode run --standalone -m MODEL` first (see Native chat verification), and expect a Cerebras/Google/Groq model whose key lives in an environment variable to fail in a worker with "Model unavailable" until that name is opted in with `AGENT_BRIDGE_PASS_ENV`. Use the lowest variant that suits a probe; a variant list is not a default. Preserve the full requested model ID; `model-guide read subscriptions` owns free variants versus Go allowances.
- **Effort**: effort selects OpenCode's model variant (`provider/model#<effort>`); omission uses the native default. Bridge reads the resolved model and variant from the session's assistant message for status and Wake. An unknown variant fails the turn with "Variant unavailable".
- **Privacy**: the free tier is limited to the zero-retention allowlist described in `model-guide read subscriptions`; read it when the choice depends on plan or retention terms. The bridge refuses any other free model and any start without `--model`. Other providers (OpenCode Go, Cerebras, Groq) follow their own terms.
- **Sandbox**: every turn requires `bwrap`; without it the runner fails closed. The filesystem is read-only except cwd and writable roots in workspace-write mode; OpenCode data is private to the job and goes with the job dir. Both modes read anywhere (OpenCode's outside-cwd check is opened; bwrap confines writes). Read-only also denies `edit`, `bash`, `webfetch` and `websearch`. A denial aborts the turn, is logged as urgent, and the worker is told to continue without it.
- **Steers** use the worker's private OpenCode server and reach an active turn at its next safe step boundary. Bridge records delivery only after the message appears in native history. `--queue` keeps a message for the next turn. Interrupt signals the active turn's process group; stop ends the runner. An unconfirmed receipt is reconciled using the same message ID on resume.
- **Sessions**: each turn owns a private server and client inside the same sandbox and resource scope. Later turns reuse the stored session ID.
- **Compact**: `agent-bridge compact <job>` starts the native compaction API for an idle session and waits for its completion or failure event. It keeps queued steers for a later resume.

`root_wake.py` detects the current `CODEX_THREAD_ID`, excluding bridge workers
and Claude roots. The independent

home's local app-server control socket and verifies `codex_tui.send_message_to_thread`
before Bridge consumes events.
At each returned event, timeout, or observer error, it opens a fresh connection
and calls the native tool for that same thread. This works after the model turn
ends; a yielded model-runtime code cell is not the adapter.

The [app-server MCP API](https://learn.chatg

After acknowledgements clear the schedule or a one-shot reminder is delivered,
the watch returns to ordinary observation; if workers remain, the original
`--timeout` deadline applies. It exits when no jobs or scheduled wakes remain,

# Epistemics

How to reason about confidence when evidence is historical, fragmentary, and sometimes contradictory, and how to tell the user without flattening it into false certainty. Code shows what it does, not *why it exists*. The why lives in commits, PRs, tickets, docs, and conversations, all incomplete, biased, and sometimes missing. Pretending otherwise produces confident-sounding guesses that mislead the user.

## Confidence Tiers

Every claim in the output must sit in one tier. The tier sets its section and its phrasing.

### 1. Direct

An explicit, textual citation answers the question: something an author actually *wrote* that says why, not "the code does X so the author must have wanted X." For example, a PR description "this fixes the bug where users with >1000 items couldn't paginate", a ticket "we're adding this because customer Acme requested it in their security review", a code comment "// clamp to 100 because the upstream API rejects larger values", a design doc "we chose option A over opti
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
most valuable outputs. The user learns the answer isn't in the obvious places, that they'll need to ask a human (the original author, the product owner, the team lead), or that they can decide the question isn't worth pursuing further. Failing to mark a gap, and instead filling it with a confident guess, actively harms the user, because they'll act on the guess. Name each gap concretely: the question, the sources searched, what you searched for in each, and what you found (nothing, or only tangential material).

## Before Finalizing

Before the synthesizer delivers the output, it checks every claim in "What We Found" and "What We Can Reasonably Infer". Each claim has a citation or moves to Inferred or Hypotheses. Its phrasing matches its tier. It doesn't treat code as evidence for its own intent (if it does, remove or reclassify it). The output has a "What We Don't Know" section. If no gaps are mentioned, that's suspicious. Either the evidence was unusually complete or something is being swept under the rug.

# Create a note

Create note lets a user save a titled note from the browser or CLI, cancel an unfinished draft, and confirm the saved note from a second user-facing view.

## Sub-features

- `create-open` opens a blank editor from each browser entry point.
- `create-save` persists a title and body.
- `create-cancel` discards an unfinished browser draft.
- `create-cli` creates the same note shape from the terminal.

## How to get to it (user POV)

- Choose the `New note` button in the browser toolbar.
- Press `n` in the browser while focus is outside an editable field.
- Run `notes create --title <title> --body <body>` in a terminal.

- No note is titled `Release checklist`.

 fill --role textbox --name "Title" --value "Discard me"`, and `control-notes browser click --role button --name "Cancel"`. The note list returns and has no `Discard me` link.
- **CLI entry.** Create a second note. Run `control-notes cli -- notes create --title "CLI note" --body "Created from terminal" --format json`. Exit code `0` and stdout contain the new note ID and title.

# Code Archaeology (git + in-repo)

## What this source contains

- Commit history (messages, dates, authors, diffs)
- PR descriptions, review comments, and discussion threads (via `gh`)
- Inline code comments, TODOs, FIXMEs, deprecation notes
- ADRs (architectural decision records) if the repo keeps them
- Tests, whose names and assertions often encode the edge cases that motivated a change
- Related files modified in the same commits (co-change signal)
- CHANGELOG entries and release notes in the repo
- Issue/ticket IDs in commit messages and PR bodies

The most trustworthy source, tied directly to the code, and the most complete. Everything that went through the repo should be here.

## How to search it

Expand the seed commit list:

```bash
# History through renames
git log --follow --oneline -- <file>

# Pickaxe: commits that added or removed this exact text
git log -S '<exact_string_from_code>' -- <file>

# Or for patterns:
git log -G '<regex>' -- <file>

# Who wrote each line and when
git blame -L <start>,<end> <file>

# One commit's full diff
git show <hash>

# Commits between two points affecting this file
git log <old>..<new> -p -- <file>
```

Look for out-of-band docs:

```bash
# ADRs often live in docs/adr/ or similar
rg -l -i 'architecture.decision' --glob '*.md'

# TODOs and FIXMEs near the target
rg -n -C2 '(TODO|FIXME|HACK|XXX|NOTE)' <target_file>

# Related tests
rg -l '<symbol>' --glob '*test*'
```

# Datadog Telemetry

## What this source contains

Datadog holds the runtime record, what actually happened in production, as opposed to what was planned or discussed.

- **Metrics.** Counters, gauges, histograms instrumented by the team. A metric's *presence* is itself evidence that someone thought the number worth watching.
- **Monitors & alerts.** Conditions the team decided warranted waking someone up. A monitor firing on `rate_limit_hit > 10/min` is direct evidence the team worried about that threshold.
- **Dashboards.** Curated views of what the team considers important for a subsystem.
- **APM traces & spans.** Request-level runtime data, for "why is this slow" / "why is there a timeout here" questions.
- **Logs.** High-volume event records, often holding the error conditions that motivated defensive code.
- **Incidents.** Formal incident records with timelines and linked postmortems.
- **Notebooks.** The team's exploratory investigations, often with hypotheses and analyses.

# Linear Tickets

## What this source contains

- Issues describing features, bugs, and their motivation
- Project docs attached to issues (often PRDs or specs)
- Parent/sub-issue relationships (broader initiative → specific tickets)
- Comments on issues (clarifications, scope changes, "why we're doing this" rationale)
- Labels (e.g., `compliance`, `customer-request`, `perf`) that signal the type of motivation
- Status updates that explain scope changes
- Attachments and linked GitHub PRs

Linear is where the product/business context often lives: the "we're doing this because customer X asked" or "this is for the Q3 compliance initiative" layer.

## How to search it

Use the Linear MCP.

1. **Start with linked tickets.** If the seed commits or PRs reference ticket IDs (e.g., `ENG-1234`, `[BUG-567]`), fetch those first with `get_issue`. Read the full issue including comments.
2. **List related issues by keyword.** Use `list_issues` with text search for the feature name, key symbol, or business term. Try multip

acme`, `incident-followup`, `compliance`, `perf-regression`

## Common pitfalls

- **Scope drift.** The ticket the PR references may have been closed and reopened with a different scope. Read the whole history.
- **Mechanical templates.** Some teams require "Why" sections but fill them with boilerplate. Generic text ("improve user experience") is probably not a real answer.
- **Stale tickets.** Old tickets often reflect a version of the plan that changed. Check dates and cross-reference with the code's ship date.
- **Closed-as-duplicate chains.** Follow the duplicate-of relationships back to the canonical ticket.
- **Private workspace content.** If you can't access an issue, note that as a gap rather than guessing.

## What to return

For each relevant ticket:
- Ticket ID and title
- The problem/motivation quoted from the description or comments (not paraphrased. The synthesizer needs the exact text to cite)
- Labels, parent issue, project
- Author, created date, closed date
- Link to the ticket if available

- PRDs (product requirement documents)
- Technical specs and RFCs
- Architectural decision records (ADRs)
- Meeting notes from design reviews
- Team pages with domain context
- Postmortems from incidents
- Runbooks that may explain defensive code

Notion is where "why" often lives in long-form before it becomes code. A significant feature usually has a doc.

Use the Notion MCP.

   - Time-bounded queries if you know when the code shipped
2. **Fetch candidate pages with `notion-fetch`.** Read the full content, not the preview. Rationale is often buried mid-document.

## Common pitfalls

- **Outdated docs.** Specs are often written before implementation and not updated. The doc may describe a plan that changed. Cross-check against the actual PR.
- **Doc vs. reality drift.** A spec may say "we'll do X" but the code actually does Y. Flag the divergence. The synthesizer will surface the contradiction.
- **Boilerplate templates.** Some orgs require a "Why" section that gets filled with fluff. Look for specificity.
- **Unlinked docs.** The most relevant doc may not be linked from anywhere. Broad keyword searches help.
- **Multiple drafts.** If a topic has multiple docs, find the one that was finalized or most recently updated. Check dates.

# Slack Conversations

## How to search it

Slack MCP tools vary. Check which Slack MCP is available and inspect its tool schema first. It may require `mcp_auth`. If authentication fails, stop and report the gap.

1. **Author-bounded search.** Messages from the PR author around the PR merge date. Limits scope dramatically and often hits gold.
3. **PR URL search.** Slack often links PRs when they're reviewed or discussed. Search for the PR URL (or just `/pull/<number>`).
4. **Error string search.** If the code handles a specific error, search for the error string. Incident threads often surface.

## Common pitfalls

- **Channel archaeology limits.** Very old messages may be gone due to retention policies. If you can't find anything before a certain date, note the retention cliff.
- **Unsearched DMs.** Many decisions happen in DMs that aren't searchable. You'll miss them. That's a known limitation.
- **Speculative jokes as "decisions."** Slack is casual. "Lol just do the thing" isn't a decision, even if it preceded the commit. Look for considered discussion.
- **Context collapse in single messages.** Without the thread, a single message often reads differently than in context. Always fetch threads.
- **Auth failures.** If the MCP isn't authenticated, stop. Don't make up findings. Report that Slack wasn't searchable.
